sources.title: Sennacherib and Jerusalem
sources.author: Ira Spar · The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.summary: The museum looks at old writings, wall pictures, and the Bible. These sources tell about the war in 701 BCE. Judah lost many towns, but Jerusalem did not fall.
sources.limitations: The museum joins several sources. We still do not know why Assyria left.
sources.license: Linked reading; original study guide summary, no article reproduction
sources.studyText: Assyrian writings and wall pictures tell about Judah’s losses. The Bible tells how Jerusalem lived. Each source has a different goal. We still do not know why Assyria left.

sources.title: Sennacherib: inscription with the Hezekiah passage
sources.author: Royal Inscriptions of the Neo-Assyrian Period, ORACC
sources.summary: Scholars edited this Assyrian royal writing and translated it. It tells of attacks on Hezekiah’s walled towns.
sources.limitations: Parts of this royal account are missing. It praises the king’s power. Its numbers and victory claims may not be exact.
sources.license: Linked reading; original study guide summary, no article reproduction
sources.studyText: The Assyrian writing tells about attacks on Judah’s walled towns. It praises the king. Part of the writing is gone. Its numbers may not be exact.

sources.title: Sennacherib receives the spoils of Lachish
sources.author: British Museum · collection 1856,0909.14
sources.summary: A relief is a picture carved on a wall. This palace relief names Lachish. It shows Assyria taking the city, as the king’s court saw it.
sources.limitations: The relief was carved after the campaign. Its pictures praise Assyria’s victory. They do not show every detail in Isaiah.

sources.title: Isaiah 36–39: rethinking priority and historical reliability
sources.author: Joel E. Anderson and Pieter M. Venter · HTS 65(1)
sources.summary: The writers compare Isaiah with the same story in Kings. They think Isaiah’s form came first. They study words that repeat and where the story was placed.
sources.limitations: Other experts do not agree. Kings may have come first. Both books may also use an older source.
sources.license: Linked reading; original study guide summary, no article reproduction
sources.studyText: Joel E. Anderson and Pieter M. Venter say Isaiah 36–39 forms one account. They say it may be older than the matching account in Kings. They connect its purpose with debate after Sennacherib’s invasion. These are scholarly views, not settled dates. They do not prove every reported event.

sources.title: My claim about Isaiah 53 is “demonstrably false”?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: McClellan says the servant is Israel. He links the servant’s pain with exile. He studies an old Aramaic Bible. He says it does not show a dying Messiah before Jesus’s time. The books he cites do not rule out every earlier idea.
sources.limitations: This video is about Isaiah 49 and 53. It gives McClellan’s view of history. It is not Church teaching. Experts still debate who the servant is. Missing proof does not prove that an idea never existed.
sources.reviewed: English auto-captions reviewed. Publication titles checked against publisher or university records.

sources.title: What is Deutero-Isaiah?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: Second Isaiah is a name for Isaiah 40–55. McClellan thinks these chapters came from a later time. Chapter 39 warns of exile. Chapter 40 speaks as if exile has begun. He also finds new words and a new style.
sources.limitations: This is one expert view. The video does not review all the proof. A new chapter does not prove that a new person wrote it. The words we checked did not name another study.
sources.reviewed: English auto-captions and video date reviewed.
sources.license: Linked resource; original study guide summary. Video, transcript, and publication text are not reproduced.

sources.title: Does the Great Isaiah Scroll prove the Bible hasn’t changed?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: McClellan compares two old Hebrew copies of Isaiah 53. Many changes are only spelling. Some changes affect the words or their meaning. One copy has the word “light” in verse 11. The text was kept well, but it did change.
sources.limitations: We did not check the video’s number totals. One chapter cannot show how much the whole Bible changed. The date of a copy is not the date when the book was first written.
sources.reviewed: English auto-captions reviewed. The cited edition’s identity and scope were checked with its publisher.
sources.license: Linked resource; original study guide summary. Video, transcript, and publication text are not reproduced.

sources.title: What’s going on with “line upon line” in Isaiah 28:10?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: Isaiah 28:10 repeats short sounds. McClellan says they copy speech that people cannot understand. Verses 11–13 warn that the people will not understand. This is not the same as a lesson about learning one step at a time.
sources.limitations: This is one way to read hard Hebrew words. A faith lesson can use the words in another way. The part we checked did not name another study.
sources.reviewed: English auto-captions and video date reviewed. No Hebrew transcription was copied from the auto-captions.

sources.title: The Glory of Israel: The Theology and Provenience of the Isaiah Targum
sources.author: Bruce D. Chilton
sources.summary: Chilton studies how the Isaiah Targum developed across the first through fourth centuries CE. A Targum is an Aramaic translation that also interprets the text. McClellan cites Chilton at 3:31 when discussing stages of interpretation around 70–135 CE. The useful distinction is between a text’s surviving form and earlier traditions within it.
sources.limitations: Publisher description and the excerpt read in the video were reviewed, not the complete book. The proposed dates describe layers of interpretation. They do not date every sentence. The linked edition’s date differs from the 1982 original cited in the video.
sources.reviewed: Publisher record checked. Video excerpt supplies the specific dating discussion.
sources.license: Linked resource; original study guide summary. Video, transcript, and publication text are not reproduced.

sources.title: The Suffering Servant between the Testaments
sources.author: S. H. T. Page
sources.summary: Page examines whether people saw the suffering servant as the Messiah before Christianity. Page rejects the claim that all readers agreed. He also refuses to rule out all earlier ideas. He finds no clear early belief in a Messiah who atones through suffering. He allows that some ideas prepared for that belief. This limit matters when we assess McClellan’s stronger opening words.
sources.limitations: Cambridge’s record, extract, and references were accessible. The conclusion was reviewed through McClellan’s reading, not a complete independent reading of the article. This 1985 study does not represent every subsequent argument.
sources.reviewed: Bibliography checked with Cambridge. The conclusion comes second-hand, through the cited video.

sources.summary: This book collects Jewish and Christian studies of Isaiah 53. McClellan introduces this book at 7:47. His selected passage describes the Targum’s victorious Messiah. sources.title: The Servant-Messiah and the Messiah’s Servants in Targum Jonathan Isaiah
sources.author: William A. Tooman
sources.year: 2021 · in Isaiah’s Servants in Early Judaism and Christianity
sources.summary: Tooman compares the traditional Hebrew text with the Isaiah Targum. The Targum presents a victorious Messiah who protects those who suffer. Its servants are the righteous who obey Torah, God’s instruction. They can include outsiders who join the covenant. This changes how the servant and the community relate. McClellan cites the chapter at 9:17.
sources.limitations: The university repository provides an accessible manuscript. Its pagination can differ from the published chapter. The argument concerns this Targum’s interpretation, not every Jewish reading of Isaiah. The university dates it to 2021. The video gave only a rough age.
sources.reviewed: Repository manuscript and University of St Andrews publication record reviewed.
sources.license: Linked resource; original study guide summary. Video, transcript, and publication text are not reproduced.

sources.title: The Biblical Qumran Scrolls: Transcriptions and Textual Variants
sources.author: Eugene Ulrich, editor
sources.summary: This edition presents written copies of Bible manuscripts from Qumran. It also records differences between the texts. McClellan introduces the edition at 1:07 in his Great Isaiah Scroll video. A critical apparatus is a set of notes about these differences. It helps readers check which manuscript supports each reading. Readers do not need to trust a broad claim about accuracy.

sources.title: Isaiah 1 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Isaiah sees a vision about Judah and Jerusalem. God says his people have left him. Their cities are burned, and strangers take their land. Jerusalem is left alone. The people still bring offerings and pray. God refuses their worship and tells them to do right. He gives them a choice: obey and eat well, or refuse and face the sword. He promises to give the city fair judges again.

sources.title: Isaiah 2 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Isaiah sees what will happen in later days. The LORD’s mountain stands above all other hills. Many peoples go up to learn his ways. He settles their disputes, and they turn swords into plow blades. Then the vision turns to Jacob’s people now. Their land is full of silver, horses, and idols. A day of the LORD will bring down every proud thing. People will throw their idols to moles and bats.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 3 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD takes bread, water, and leaders away from Jerusalem and Judah. Soldiers, judges, prophets, and elders are gone. Boys rule, and neighbors hurt each other. One man begs his brother to rule the ruin, and the brother refuses. Then the LORD stands up as judge. He charges the elders and leaders with robbing the poor. He also says the proud women of Zion will lose their fine things. The city gates mourn, and the men fall in war.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 4 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Verse 1 ends the war scene from chapter 3. So few men are left that seven women ask one man for his name. Then the picture changes. The LORD’s branch and the land’s fruit become the pride of the survivors. Those left in Jerusalem are called holy. The Lord washes the city’s filth and blood away with justice and burning. He covers Mount Zion with cloud by day and fire by night. A shelter gives shade from heat and cover from storm.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 5 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: A singer begins a love song about a friend’s vineyard. The owner dug, cleared stones, planted good vines, and built a tower. The vines gave wild grapes. The owner asks Judah to judge, then says he will break down its wall. Verse 7 names the vineyard: Israel and Judah. Six cries of “Woe” name land grabbers, heavy drinkers, and judges who take bribes. The LORD’s anger burns, and his hand stays stretched out. He whistles for a far nation, and its army comes fast.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 6 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Isaiah tells what he saw in the year King Uzziah died. The Lord sits on a high throne in the temple. Six-winged beings called seraphim call out, “Holy, holy, holy.” The doorposts shake, and smoke fills the house. Isaiah says he is ruined because his lips are unclean. A seraph touches his mouth with a hot coal and says his sin is forgiven. The Lord asks whom to send, and Isaiah offers to go. His message will not be understood until the land lies empty.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 7 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The kings of Syria and Israel march against King Ahaz in Jerusalem. Ahaz and his people shake with fear. The LORD sends Isaiah and his son to meet Ahaz by the upper pool. Isaiah says the two kings are only smoking stubs, and their plan will fail. The LORD offers Ahaz a sign, but Ahaz refuses to ask. Isaiah gives one anyway: the virgin will bear a son named Immanuel. Before the boy can choose good, both enemy lands will be empty. Then the LORD will bring the king of Assyria on Judah.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 8 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Isaiah writes the name Maher Shalal Hash Baz on a large tablet. The prophetess bears Isaiah a son, and the boy gets that name. Before the boy can talk, Assyria will plunder Damascus and Samaria. The people refused the quiet waters of Shiloah. So the king of Assyria will come like a flood, up to Judah’s neck. The LORD warns Isaiah not to share the people’s fears. Isaiah seals the teaching among his followers and waits. People who ask the dead for help will find only darkness.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 9 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The gloom over Zebulun and Naphtali ends. People who walked in darkness see a great light. The oppressor’s rod breaks, and armor and bloody clothes burn. A child is born who will rule on David’s throne. His names include Wonderful Counselor and Prince of Peace. Then the word turns against Israel and Samaria. They boast that they will rebuild with cut stone. Enemies, lying leaders, and fighting between tribes follow, and the LORD’s hand stays stretched out.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 10 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The chapter opens with woe to lawmakers who rob widows and the fatherless. Then the LORD calls Assyria the rod of his anger. He sends Assyria against a people who anger him. But Assyria’s king plans to destroy many nations and boasts of his own strength. The LORD will punish that pride after his work on Jerusalem. A remnant of Israel will return and lean on the LORD. An army marches town by town toward Jerusalem. Then the LORD cuts down the tall trees.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 11 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: A shoot grows from the stock of Jesse. The LORD’s Spirit rests on him with wisdom, counsel, and might. He does not judge by what he sees or hears. He judges the poor with fairness and strikes the wicked with his words. Wolf and lamb, cow and bear, child and snake live without harm. The nations look for this root of Jesse. The Lord gathers his scattered people from Assyria, Egypt, and far lands. Ephraim and Judah stop fighting each other, and a road opens for those who return.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 12 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: This chapter is a short song for “that day.” The singer thanks the LORD because his anger has turned away. The singer says, “God is my salvation,” and will trust without fear. The people draw water with joy from the wells of salvation. They tell the nations what the LORD has done. Zion is told to shout, because the Holy One of Israel is great among them.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 13 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Isaiah sees a message about Babylon. A banner goes up, and the LORD gathers an army from far lands. The day of the LORD comes with anger. Hands go weak, hearts melt, and the sun, moon, and stars go dark. The LORD says he will punish evil and end the pride of the proud. He stirs up the Medes, who do not care for silver or gold. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, will fall like Sodom and Gomorrah. Only wild animals will live there.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 14 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD will have compassion on Jacob and settle Israel in its own land. Then Israel will sing a taunt against the king of Babylon. The whole earth rests and sings. Dead kings in Sheol, the place of the dead, say he is weak like them. He said he would rise above the stars. He is thrown out without a tomb. The LORD also swears to break Assyria in his land. A last message warns Philistia not to rejoice.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 15 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: This is a message about Moab. Two Moabite cities, Ar and Kir, fall in one night. People go up to the high places to weep. They shave their heads, cut their beards, and wear rough sackcloth. The cry spreads from town to town, and soldiers shake. The speaker says, “My heart cries out for Moab!” Nobles flee to Zoar, weeping as they climb. The waters dry up or run with blood, and more trouble is coming.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 16 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Moab is told to send lambs to the ruler on Mount Zion. Moab’s women are like birds pushed from a nest at the Arnon river crossings. A voice asks for shelter: hide the outcasts and do not betray them. A throne will stand in David’s tent, with a judge who seeks justice. But Moab’s pride is well known, and its boasts are empty. Its vines and harvest songs stop, and the speaker weeps for them. Moab’s prayers at its high place will not work. Within three years its glory will be small.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 17 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: This is a message about Damascus. Damascus will stop being a city and become a heap of ruins. Ephraim loses its fortress too. Jacob’s glory grows thin, like a field after harvest. Only a few olives stay on the highest branches. In that day people will look to their Maker, not to altars they made. They forgot the God who saved them, so their planting gives no harvest. Many nations roar like the sea, but by morning they are gone.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 18 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The message speaks to a land beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. It sends messengers in papyrus boats. They go to a tall, smooth people whose land the rivers divide. All the world is told to watch for a banner and listen for a trumpet. The LORD says he will stay still and watch, like heat in sunshine. Before the harvest he cuts off the branches and leaves them for birds and animals. Then that tall people will bring a gift to the LORD at Mount Zion.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 19 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: This is a message about Egypt. The LORD rides a swift cloud to Egypt, and its idols shake. Egyptians fight each other, and a cruel king rules them. The Nile dries up, and fishermen and weavers lose their work. Pharaoh’s wise men give foolish advice. Then five Egyptian cities swear to the LORD, and an altar to him stands there. The LORD strikes Egypt and heals it. A highway joins Egypt and Assyria, and the LORD blesses both with Israel.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 20 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Assyria’s commander takes the city of Ashdod for King Sargon. At that time the LORD tells Isaiah to take off his sackcloth and sandals. Isaiah walks naked and barefoot for three years. The LORD says this is a sign about Egypt and Ethiopia. Assyria’s king will lead their captives away the same way, young and old. People who trusted Egypt and Ethiopia will be ashamed. The people of the coast will ask how they can escape.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 21 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Three short messages follow. In the first, Isaiah sees a hard vision and shakes with pain. A watchman stands at his post day and night. He sees riders in pairs and hears, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon.” In the second, a voice from Seir asks the watchman about the night. He answers that morning comes, and also night. In the third, people of Tema bring water and bread to those fleeing battle. Within a year the glory of Kedar will fail.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 22 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: This message is about the “valley of vision,” and it speaks to Jerusalem. The people are on the rooftops shouting, but their rulers fled and were captured. The speaker weeps for the city. Enemy chariots fill the valleys. The people check weapons, break down houses to fix the wall, and store water. They do not look to the one who planned it. They feast and say, “Let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die.” Then Shebna the palace manager loses his place to Eliakim.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 23 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: This is a message about Tyre. Ships of Tarshish are told to howl, because Tyre’s harbor and houses are gone. Tyre was the market of nations, and grain from the Nile made it rich. Its traders were like princes. Who planned its fall? The LORD of Armies planned it, to shame the pride of all glory. Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years. Then it trades again, and its earnings feed those who live before the LORD.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 24 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD empties the earth and scatters its people. Priest and people, master and servant, lender and borrower all share the same end. The earth mourns because its people broke the laws and the everlasting covenant. Wine, music, and joy stop, and the city is broken. A few remain, like olives after shaking, and they sing from far coasts. The speaker still cries, “Woe is me!” The earth sways like a drunk man and falls. The LORD punishes powers above and kings below, and he reigns on Mount Zion.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 25 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The speaker praises the LORD for wonderful things planned long ago. The LORD turned a strong city into a heap. He has been a stronghold for the poor and shade from the heat. On this mountain he will make a rich feast for all peoples. He will destroy the veil that covers all nations. He swallows up death forever and wipes tears from all faces. The people say they waited for this God, and he will save them. Moab’s pride is brought down to the dust.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 26 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Judah will sing this song in that day. The singers have a strong city, and salvation is its walls. The LORD keeps a steady mind in peace because it trusts him. He brought the high city down, and the feet of the poor walk on it. The singers say they waited for the LORD through the night. Other lords ruled them, and their own efforts gave birth only to wind. Then comes a promise: “Your dead shall live.” The people are told to hide a little while until the anger passes.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 27 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: In that day the LORD kills leviathan, the twisting serpent of the sea. In a new vineyard song, the LORD keeps the vineyard and waters it. He says he has no anger. Thorns may be burned or may make peace with him. Jacob will take root, and Israel will fill the world with fruit. Jacob’s sin is forgiven when the altar stones are crushed like chalk. The strong city lies empty. A great trumpet calls the lost from Assyria and Egypt to worship in Jerusalem.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 28 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Woe comes to Ephraim’s drunk leaders, whose crown is a fading flower. A strong one from the Lord will throw it down like a hailstorm. Priests and prophets stagger with drink too. They ask if the teaching is for small children: “line on line, here a little.” Jerusalem’s rulers say they made a covenant with death. The Lord GOD lays a tested cornerstone in Zion and measures with justice. Hail will sweep away their shelter of lies. A farmer does not plow or thresh forever, and this wisdom comes from the LORD.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 29 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Woe comes to Ariel, the city where David camped. The LORD will camp against it, and its voice will whisper from the dust. Then its enemies blow away like chaff, like a dream after waking. The prophets are in a deep sleep, and the vision is like a sealed book. The Lord says this people honors him with lips while their hearts are far away. He will do a wonder, and the wisdom of the wise will fail. In a little while the deaf will hear and the blind will see. The humble will rejoice, and Jacob will no longer be ashamed.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 30 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD says woe to rebellious children who go to Egypt without asking him. Their envoys carry treasure through a desert, but Egypt’s help is empty. The people tell the prophets to say only pleasant things. So their sin is like a bulging wall that breaks at once. The Lord GOD offered rescue through returning and rest, and they refused. Still the LORD waits to be gracious. A voice will say, “This is the way.” He will heal his people and strike Assyria with his rod.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 31 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Woe comes to those who go down to Egypt for help. They trust many chariots and strong horsemen and do not seek the LORD. The Egyptians are men and not God, and their horses are flesh. When the LORD stretches out his hand, helper and helped fall together. The LORD will fight for Mount Zion like a lion over its prey. He will guard Jerusalem like hovering birds. Israel is called to return and throw away its idols. The Assyrian will fall by a sword that is not a man’s.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 32 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: A king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice. Each will be like shelter from wind and water in a dry place. Eyes will see, ears will listen, and fools will no longer be called noble. Then the speaker warns the women who feel safe. In little more than a year the grape harvest will fail. Thorns will grow, and the palace and city will be empty. This lasts until the Spirit is poured out from on high. Then justice lives in the land, and its fruit is peace and safe homes.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 33 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Woe comes to a destroyer who has not yet been destroyed. The people ask the LORD to be gracious, because they have waited for him. Envoys of peace weep, the roads are empty, and the land withers. The LORD says, “Now I will arise.” Sinners in Zion ask who can live with the burning fire. The answer is one who walks rightly, refuses bribes, and turns from bloodshed. That person will see the king and a quiet Jerusalem. The LORD is judge, lawgiver, and king, and he will save.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 34 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: All nations are called to listen. The LORD is angry with the nations and their armies. The sky rolls up like a scroll, and its stars fade like leaves. His sword comes down on Edom, with a great slaughter at Bozrah. The LORD has a day of vengeance for Zion’s cause. Edom’s streams turn to pitch, and its smoke rises forever. Owls, ravens, jackals, and snakes take over its palaces. The LORD’s book says not one of these animals will be missing.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 35 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The desert will be glad and bloom. It will see the glory of the LORD. Weak hands and shaking knees are to be made strong. The fearful are told that God will come and save them. Then the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, and the mute sing. Water breaks out in the dry land. A road called the Holy Way runs through it, and no lion is there. The LORD’s ransomed people come to Zion singing, and sorrow flees.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 40 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: God says, “Comfort, comfort my people.” Jerusalem’s hard service is over, and her sin is pardoned. A voice calls for a level road in the desert for the LORD. Another voice says people are like grass, but God’s word stands forever. Zion is told to say, “Behold, your God!” He comes with power and carries lambs like a shepherd. No one taught him, and no nation or idol compares with him. Jacob says God has missed his case, yet those who wait gain new strength.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 41 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD calls the far coasts to meet him in court. He asks who raised up a conqueror from the east. The answer is the LORD, the first and with the last. The nations are afraid, and their workers nail idols down so they will not fall. The LORD calls Israel his servant, chosen and not thrown away. He tells Israel not to fear, because he will help and hold it up. He will give water to the poor and trees to the desert. He dares the idols to tell the future, and they cannot.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 42 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD presents his servant and puts his Spirit on him. The servant brings justice to the nations without shouting in the street. He does not break a bruised reed or put out a weak wick. He is a light for the nations, to open blind eyes and free prisoners. All the earth is called to sing a new song. The LORD, long silent, goes out like a warrior and leads the blind. Then he calls his own servant blind and deaf. Israel was robbed because it would not walk in his ways.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 43 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD who made Jacob says not to fear. He has redeemed Israel, called it by name, and says, “You are mine.” He will be with them through water and fire. He will gather their children from east, west, north, and south. The nations are called to court, and Israel is the LORD’s witness. For Israel’s sake he sends to Babylon. He is doing a new thing: a road and rivers in the desert. Israel wore him out with sins, yet he blots them out for his own sake.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 44 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD tells Jacob his servant not to fear. He will pour water on dry ground and his Spirit on their children. He is the first and the last, and there is no other God. Then the chapter describes an idol maker. He burns half a tree to cook and bows to the other half. No one stops to think that it is a block of wood. The LORD tells Israel he has wiped out its sins like a cloud. He says Jerusalem will be built, and he names Cyrus as his shepherd.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 45 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD speaks to Cyrus, his anointed, and holds his right hand. He will open gates before Cyrus and give him hidden treasure. He does this for Jacob’s sake, though Cyrus has not known him. The LORD says he forms light and darkness, peace and trouble. Woe comes to anyone who argues with his Maker, like clay with a potter. Cyrus will build the city and free the exiles without payment. The LORD did not speak in secret. He calls all the ends of the earth to look to him and be saved.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 46 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Bel and Nebo bow down. Animals carry their idols as heavy loads, and the idols go into captivity. The LORD tells Jacob’s house that he has carried them from birth. He will carry them to old age and gray hair. People pay a goldsmith to make a god, then lift it on their shoulders. It stands where they set it and cannot answer. The LORD declares the end from the beginning. He calls a bird of prey from the east and brings salvation to Zion.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 47 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Babylon is told to come down and sit in the dust. She will grind flour at the millstones and be called tender no more. The LORD says he gave his people into her hand, and she showed no mercy. She laid a heavy yoke even on the old. She said, “I will be a princess forever.” In one day she will lose both children and husband. Her spells and star readers cannot save her. They burn like stubble, and no one is left to help.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 48 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD speaks to Jacob’s house, who swear by his name but not in truth. He told them things long ago so they could not credit an idol. Now he tells new things they have not heard. He holds back his anger for his own name’s sake. He has tested them in the furnace of suffering. He says their peace would have been like a river if they had listened. Then the order comes: leave Babylon and shout that the LORD has redeemed Jacob. There is no peace for the wicked.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 49 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The servant speaks to far peoples. The LORD called him before birth and made his mouth like a sharp sword. The servant says he has worked for nothing, yet his reward is with God. The LORD says restoring Israel is too small a task. The servant will be a light to the nations. Captives will come out and be led by springs of water. Zion says the LORD has forgotten her. He answers that a mother may forget her baby, but he will not forget Zion.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 50 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD asks for the divorce paper and the name of any lender he owed. He says the people were sold for their own sins. He asks why no one answered when he called. Then a servant speaks. The Lord GOD wakes his ear each morning and gives him words for the weary. He gave his back to those who beat him and did not hide from spitting. He sets his face like flint, because the Lord GOD will help him. Those who fear the LORD are told to trust him in the dark.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 51 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD speaks to those who seek him. Look to Abraham and Sarah, he says: Abraham was one, and God made him many. The LORD will comfort Zion and make her desert like Eden. The sky will fade like smoke, but his salvation lasts forever. A voice calls the LORD’s arm to wake, as when it dried the sea. The LORD asks why they fear men who die like grass. Jerusalem has drunk the cup of his anger to the bottom. He takes the cup from her hand and gives it to those who hurt her.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 52 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Zion is told to wake, put on fine clothes, and shake off the dust. The LORD says she was sold for nothing and will be bought back without money. His people were taken away, and his name is mocked all day. So they will know his name. A messenger runs on the mountains with good news: “Your God reigns!” The watchmen sing as the LORD returns to Zion. The people leave without rushing, with the LORD ahead and behind. The LORD says his marred servant will be lifted very high.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 53 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: A group speaks and asks who has believed their message. The servant grew like a root in dry ground, with no beauty to draw them. People despised him, and the speakers did not respect him. They thought God was striking him. But he carried their sickness and was pierced for their wrongs. Like a silent lamb, he did not open his mouth. He was cut off and buried with the wicked, though he had done no violence. After his suffering he will see light, and he will make many righteous.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 54 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: A woman with no children is told to sing. She will have many children, so she must make her tent bigger. She will forget the shame of her youth. Her Maker is her husband and her Redeemer. He left her for a short moment and gathers her with great mercy. As he swore about Noah’s flood, he swears not to be angry with her. He will rebuild her with jewels, and the LORD will teach her children. No weapon made against her will succeed.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 55 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD calls everyone who is thirsty to come to the water. Those with no money may buy wine and milk without price. He asks why they spend money on what is not bread. If they listen, they will live, and he will make a lasting covenant with them. They should seek the LORD while he is near and return for pardon. His thoughts are higher than theirs, as the sky is above the earth. His word is like rain: it does what he sends it to do. They will go out with joy, and the trees will clap.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 56 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD says to keep justice, because his salvation is near. The one who keeps the Sabbath and does no evil is blessed. A foreigner should not say the LORD will shut him out. A eunuch, a man who cannot father children, should not call himself a dry tree. The LORD will give faithful eunuchs a name better than sons and daughters. He will bring foreigners who hold to his covenant to his holy mountain. His house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples. But Israel’s watchmen are blind, like dogs that cannot bark.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 57 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Good people die, and no one thinks about it. They enter peace. Then the LORD charges others with worship under trees and killing children in the valleys. They set their bed on a high mountain and sent envoys far away. Their collected idols cannot save them, and a breath will carry them off. A voice says to clear the road for God’s people. The high and holy One says he also lives with the humble. He will not be angry forever and will heal, but the wicked have no peace.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 58 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD tells the speaker to shout Israel’s sins like a trumpet. The people seek him daily and ask why he ignores their fasts. He answers that on fast days they push their workers and fight. Bowing the head like a reed is not the fast he chose. His fast is to free the oppressed and break every yoke. It is to feed the hungry, house the poor, and clothe the naked. Then their light will break out, and he will answer, “Here I am.” If they honor the Sabbath, they will delight in the LORD.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 59 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD’s hand is not too short to save, and his ear can hear. The people’s sins have come between them and God. Their hands shed blood, their lips lie, and no one goes to court honestly. Then the people speak: they look for light and walk in darkness. They admit that truth has fallen in the street. The LORD sees that there is no justice and no one to step in. So his own arm saves, and he puts on righteousness like armor. A Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from wrong.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 60 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: Zion is told to rise and shine, because her light has come. Darkness covers the earth, but the LORD’s glory rises on her. Nations and kings come to her light. Her sons and daughters come home from far away. Camels bring gold and frankincense, and ships bring her children. Foreigners rebuild her walls, and her gates stay open day and night. Peace and righteousness will rule her, and violence will end. The LORD will be her lasting light in place of sun and moon.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 61 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: A speaker says the Lord GOD’s Spirit is on him. The LORD has anointed him to bring good news to the humble. He is sent to heal broken hearts and announce freedom to captives. He proclaims the year of the LORD’s favor and comforts those who mourn. They get a garland in place of ashes and will rebuild old ruins. They will be called the LORD’s priests. The LORD says he loves justice and will make a lasting covenant with them. The speaker rejoices, clothed in salvation like a bride or groom.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 62 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The speaker will not keep quiet until Zion’s righteousness shines like dawn. Nations and kings will see it, and the LORD will give her a new name. She will no longer be called Forsaken, or her land Desolate. Her new names are Hephzibah and Beulah, because the LORD delights in her. God will rejoice over her as a groom over a bride. Watchmen on the walls must give the LORD no rest. He swears that enemies will no longer eat her grain. The people will be called the Holy People, the LORD’s Redeemed.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 63 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: A watcher asks who comes from Edom in red clothes. The one coming says he trod the wine press alone, in anger, with no helper. Then a speaker recalls the LORD’s loving kindness to Israel. He became their Savior and carried them in the old days. But they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, and he fought against them. The people remember Moses and the sea. They ask God to look down, calling him “our Father.” They ask why enemies have trampled his holy place.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 64 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The prayer goes on. The people ask God to tear the heavens and come down, as he once did. No eye has seen a God like him, who works for those who wait. They confess long sin and ask, “Shall we be saved?” All their right acts are like a dirty cloth, and they fade like leaves. No one calls on his name. Still they call him Father and potter, and themselves clay. Zion is a wilderness, the temple is burned, and they ask for an answer.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 65 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD says he let himself be found by people who did not seek him. All day he held out his hands to a rebellious people. They offer sacrifices in gardens, sit among graves, and eat pig’s meat. He will repay them, yet he spares some, like a good grape cluster. His servants will eat and sing, and those who left him will go hungry. Then he says he creates new heavens and a new earth. People will build houses and live in them, and plant vineyards and eat. Wolf and lamb will feed together.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

sources.title: Isaiah 66 — World English Bible
sources.author: World English Bible project
sources.summary: The LORD says heaven is his throne and earth his footstool. He asks what house people could build for him. He looks to the one who is poor, sorry, and trembles at his word. He rejects offerings from those who choose their own ways. Zion gives birth to a nation in one day, before her pain comes. The LORD will comfort Jerusalem as a mother comforts her child. He comes with fire to judge, and gathers all nations to see his glory. All flesh will worship him, and the rebels’ bodies lie outside.
sources.limitations: This source gives the Bible text. The notes and questions are original study material. The notes are study help, not proof from history.

passages.title: Worship and justice
passages.summary: Isaiah sees a vision about Judah and Jerusalem. God says his people have left him. Their cities are burned, and strangers take their land. Jerusalem is left alone. The people still bring offerings and pray. God refuses their worship and tells them to do right. He gives them a choice: obey and eat well, or refuse and face the sword. He promises to give the city fair judges again.

lds.text: God refuses prayers from people who harm others. What do verses 16–17 tell them to do?

studyNotes.title: Ann Madsen on three images of an isolated city
studyNotes.text: Ann N. Madsen is a Latter-day Saint Isaiah scholar. In an interview, she explains how Isaiah 1:8 uses related images. They develop one idea. A temporary field shelter and a city under attack show different parts of Zion’s isolation. The lines build meaning through comparison, not end rhyme.
studyNotes.application: Read verses 7–9 together. The images follow the account of ruined land; the surviving city remains exposed. Survival here does not mean safety.

passages.title: Nations learn peace
passages.summary: Isaiah sees what will happen in later days. The LORD’s mountain stands above all other hills. Many peoples go up to learn his ways. He settles their disputes, and they turn swords into plow blades. Then the vision turns to Jacob’s people now. Their land is full of silver, horses, and idols. A day of the LORD will bring down every proud thing. People will throw their idols to moles and bats.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The nations ask to learn the LORD’s ways (verse 3). What do they give up in verse 4?

studyNotes.title: Hopkin: compare the wording before the commentary
studyNotes.text: Hopkin puts the scripture texts first. Parallel columns let readers see differences directly, while brief notes help with difficult points.
studyNotes.application: Compare Isaiah 2:16 in the King James Version with 2 Nephi 12:16. Both name ships of Tarshish. The Book of Mormon also names ships of the sea. Mark the extra words. Then read verses 12–17. The list leads to the humbling of human pride. This example applies Hopkin’s method. He does not discuss this verse in the interview.

passages.title: Leadership and responsibility
passages.summary: The LORD takes bread, water, and leaders away from Jerusalem and Judah. Soldiers, judges, prophets, and elders are gone. Boys rule, and neighbors hurt each other. One man begs his brother to rule the ruin, and the brother refuses. Then the LORD stands up as judge. He charges the elders and leaders with robbing the poor. He also says the proud women of Zion will lose their fine things. The city gates mourn, and the men fall in war.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD asks leaders why they “crush my people” (verse 15). What does verse 14 say is in their houses?

passages.title: Cleansing and shelter
passages.summary: Verse 1 ends the war scene from chapter 3. So few men are left that seven women ask one man for his name. Then the picture changes. The LORD’s branch and the land’s fruit become the pride of the survivors. Those left in Jerusalem are called holy. The Lord washes the city’s filth and blood away with justice and burning. He covers Mount Zion with cloud by day and fire by night. A shelter gives shade from heat and cover from storm.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The city is washed in verse 4 and sheltered in verse 6. Why does the washing come first?

passages.title: The vineyard and its fruit
passages.summary: A singer begins a love song about a friend’s vineyard. The owner dug, cleared stones, planted good vines, and built a tower. The vines gave wild grapes. The owner asks Judah to judge, then says he will break down its wall. Verse 7 names the vineyard: Israel and Judah. Six cries of “Woe” name land grabbers, heavy drinkers, and judges who take bribes. The LORD’s anger burns, and his hand stays stretched out. He whistles for a far nation, and its army comes fast.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The owner asks what more he could have done (verse 4). What did he expect to find in verse 7?

passages.title: Isaiah's call
passages.summary: Isaiah tells what he saw in the year King Uzziah died. The Lord sits on a high throne in the temple. Six-winged beings called seraphim call out, “Holy, holy, holy.” The doorposts shake, and smoke fills the house. Isaiah says he is ruined because his lips are unclean. A seraph touches his mouth with a hot coal and says his sin is forgiven. The Lord asks whom to send, and Isaiah offers to go. His message will not be understood until the land lies empty.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Isaiah says “Send me” before he hears the task. What does the Lord tell him in verses 9–12?

studyNotes.title: Ann Madsen on Isaiah’s offer to serve
studyNotes.text: Latter-day Saint Isaiah scholar Ann N. Madsen explains in an interview that hineni in Isaiah 6:8 expresses readiness to serve. Isaiah offers himself for the mission; he does more than announce his presence.
studyNotes.application: Trace the steps in verses 5–8. Isaiah admits his unclean lips. He receives cleansing and then volunteers. His offer follows the removal of guilt. Read the reply as a response to that cleansing.

passages.title: Ahaz faces a threat
passages.summary: The kings of Syria and Israel march against King Ahaz in Jerusalem. Ahaz and his people shake with fear. The LORD sends Isaiah and his son to meet Ahaz by the upper pool. Isaiah says the two kings are only smoking stubs, and their plan will fail. The LORD offers Ahaz a sign, but Ahaz refuses to ask. Isaiah gives one anyway: the virgin will bear a son named Immanuel. Before the boy can choose good, both enemy lands will be empty. Then the LORD will bring the king of Assyria on Judah.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Ahaz is told to keep calm and believe (verses 4 and 9). What does he do when offered a sign?

passages.title: Signs and competing voices
passages.summary: Isaiah writes the name Maher Shalal Hash Baz on a large tablet. The prophetess bears Isaiah a son, and the boy gets that name. Before the boy can talk, Assyria will plunder Damascus and Samaria. The people refused the quiet waters of Shiloah. So the king of Assyria will come like a flood, up to Judah’s neck. The LORD warns Isaiah not to share the people’s fears. Isaiah seals the teaching among his followers and waits. People who ask the dead for help will find only darkness.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The people fear two kings. What does verse 14 say the LORD becomes for those who fear him?

passages.title: Light and a just ruler
passages.summary: The gloom over Zebulun and Naphtali ends. People who walked in darkness see a great light. The oppressor’s rod breaks, and armor and bloody clothes burn. A child is born who will rule on David’s throne. His names include Wonderful Counselor and Prince of Peace. Then the word turns against Israel and Samaria. They boast that they will rebuild with cut stone. Enemies, lying leaders, and fighting between tribes follow, and the LORD’s hand stays stretched out.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Verse 7 says the child rules with justice and righteousness. Who does the verse say will make this happen?

passages.title: Assyria and the remnant
passages.summary: The chapter opens with woe to lawmakers who rob widows and the fatherless. Then the LORD calls Assyria the rod of his anger. He sends Assyria against a people who anger him. But Assyria’s king plans to destroy many nations and boasts of his own strength. The LORD will punish that pride after his work on Jerusalem. A remnant of Israel will return and lean on the LORD. An army marches town by town toward Jerusalem. Then the LORD cuts down the tall trees.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Assyria’s king says his own hand did it (verse 13). How does verse 15 answer him?

passages.title: A ruler from Jesse's line
passages.summary: A shoot grows from the stock of Jesse. The LORD’s Spirit rests on him with wisdom, counsel, and might. He does not judge by what he sees or hears. He judges the poor with fairness and strikes the wicked with his words. Wolf and lamb, cow and bear, child and snake live without harm. The nations look for this root of Jesse. The Lord gathers his scattered people from Assyria, Egypt, and far lands. Ephraim and Judah stop fighting each other, and a road opens for those who return.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: This king does not judge by what he sees or hears (verse 3). Who gains from that in verse 4?

passages.title: Songs of salvation
passages.summary: This chapter is a short song for “that day.” The singer thanks the LORD because his anger has turned away. The singer says, “God is my salvation,” and will trust without fear. The people draw water with joy from the wells of salvation. They tell the nations what the LORD has done. Zion is told to shout, because the Holy One of Israel is great among them.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The singer says, “I will trust, and will not be afraid” (verse 2). What had changed in verse 1?

passages.title: Judgment on Babylon
passages.summary: Isaiah sees a message about Babylon. A banner goes up, and the LORD gathers an army from far lands. The day of the LORD comes with anger. Hands go weak, hearts melt, and the sun, moon, and stars go dark. The LORD says he will punish evil and end the pride of the proud. He stirs up the Medes, who do not care for silver or gold. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, will fall like Sodom and Gomorrah. Only wild animals will live there.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Verse 19 calls Babylon “the glory of kingdoms.” What does verse 11 say the LORD will do to the proud?

passages.title: A fallen king
passages.summary: The LORD will have compassion on Jacob and settle Israel in its own land. Then Israel will sing a taunt against the king of Babylon. The whole earth rests and sings. Dead kings in Sheol, the place of the dead, say he is weak like them. He said he would rise above the stars. He is thrown out without a tomb. The LORD also swears to break Assyria in his land. A last message warns Philistia not to rejoice.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The king said, “I will make myself like the Most High” (verse 14). Where does verse 15 say he goes?

passages.title: Mourning for Moab
passages.summary: This is a message about Moab. Two Moabite cities, Ar and Kir, fall in one night. People go up to the high places to weep. They shave their heads, cut their beards, and wear rough sackcloth. The cry spreads from town to town, and soldiers shake. The speaker says, “My heart cries out for Moab!” Nobles flee to Zoar, weeping as they climb. The waters dry up or run with blood, and more trouble is coming.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The speaker’s heart “cries out for Moab” (verse 5). Why does a message of judgment include grief? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Refuge and Moab's pride
passages.summary: Moab is told to send lambs to the ruler on Mount Zion. Moab’s women are like birds pushed from a nest at the Arnon river crossings. A voice asks for shelter: hide the outcasts and do not betray them. A throne will stand in David’s tent, with a judge who seeks justice. But Moab’s pride is well known, and its boasts are empty. Its vines and harvest songs stop, and the speaker weeps for them. Moab’s prayers at its high place will not work. Within three years its glory will be small.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Moab’s outcasts ask for a hiding place (verses 3–4). What kind of ruler does verse 5 describe? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Damascus and Israel
passages.summary: This is a message about Damascus. Damascus will stop being a city and become a heap of ruins. Ephraim loses its fortress too. Jacob’s glory grows thin, like a field after harvest. Only a few olives stay on the highest branches. In that day people will look to their Maker, not to altars they made. They forgot the God who saved them, so their planting gives no harvest. Many nations roar like the sea, but by morning they are gone.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: People look to their Maker and not to what their fingers made (verses 7–8). What had they forgotten in verse 10? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Messengers from Cush
passages.summary: The message speaks to a land beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. It sends messengers in papyrus boats. They go to a tall, smooth people whose land the rivers divide. All the world is told to watch for a banner and listen for a trumpet. The LORD says he will stay still and watch, like heat in sunshine. Before the harvest he cuts off the branches and leaves them for birds and animals. Then that tall people will bring a gift to the LORD at Mount Zion.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD says, “I will be still, and I will see” (verse 4). What happens before the harvest in verse 5? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Egypt, Assyria, and Israel
passages.summary: This is a message about Egypt. The LORD rides a swift cloud to Egypt, and its idols shake. Egyptians fight each other, and a cruel king rules them. The Nile dries up, and fishermen and weavers lose their work. Pharaoh’s wise men give foolish advice. Then five Egyptian cities swear to the LORD, and an altar to him stands there. The LORD strikes Egypt and heals it. A highway joins Egypt and Assyria, and the LORD blesses both with Israel.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD calls Egypt “my people” (verse 25). What does verse 22 say he does before that? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: A sign against reliance on Egypt
passages.summary: Assyria’s commander takes the city of Ashdod for King Sargon. At that time the LORD tells Isaiah to take off his sackcloth and sandals. Isaiah walks naked and barefoot for three years. The LORD says this is a sign about Egypt and Ethiopia. Assyria’s king will lead their captives away the same way, young and old. People who trusted Egypt and Ethiopia will be ashamed. The people of the coast will ask how they can escape.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The coast people fled to Egypt for help (verse 6). What does Isaiah’s sign show them about Egypt? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Watchmen and warnings
passages.summary: Three short messages follow. In the first, Isaiah sees a hard vision and shakes with pain. A watchman stands at his post day and night. He sees riders in pairs and hears, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon.” In the second, a voice from Seir asks the watchman about the night. He answers that morning comes, and also night. In the third, people of Tema bring water and bread to those fleeing battle. Within a year the glory of Kedar will fail.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Tema’s people meet the fugitives with water and bread (verse 14). What were the fugitives running from in verse 15? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Jerusalem under scrutiny
passages.summary: This message is about the “valley of vision,” and it speaks to Jerusalem. The people are on the rooftops shouting, but their rulers fled and were captured. The speaker weeps for the city. Enemy chariots fill the valleys. The people check weapons, break down houses to fix the wall, and store water. They do not look to the one who planned it. They feast and say, “Let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die.” Then Shebna the palace manager loses his place to Eliakim.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The city fixes its walls and stores water (verses 9–11). What does verse 11 say the people left out?

passages.title: Tyre and the sea trade
passages.summary: This is a message about Tyre. Ships of Tarshish are told to howl, because Tyre’s harbor and houses are gone. Tyre was the market of nations, and grain from the Nile made it rich. Its traders were like princes. Who planned its fall? The LORD of Armies planned it, to shame the pride of all glory. Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years. Then it trades again, and its earnings feed those who live before the LORD.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Tyre’s traders were “the honorable of the earth” (verse 8). What does verse 9 say the LORD planned for that honor? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: The earth brought low
passages.summary: The LORD empties the earth and scatters its people. Priest and people, master and servant, lender and borrower all share the same end. The earth mourns because its people broke the laws and the everlasting covenant. Wine, music, and joy stop, and the city is broken. A few remain, like olives after shaking, and they sing from far coasts. The speaker still cries, “Woe is me!” The earth sways like a drunk man and falls. The LORD punishes powers above and kings below, and he reigns on Mount Zion.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Verse 5 says the earth is polluted “under its inhabitants.” What three things does the verse say they did?

passages.title: A feast and the end of death
passages.summary: The speaker praises the LORD for wonderful things planned long ago. The LORD turned a strong city into a heap. He has been a stronghold for the poor and shade from the heat. On this mountain he will make a rich feast for all peoples. He will destroy the veil that covers all nations. He swallows up death forever and wipes tears from all faces. The people say they waited for this God, and he will save them. Moab’s pride is brought down to the dust.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Sheol opens its mouth for people in 5:14. What does the LORD swallow in 25:8?

passages.title: Trust while waiting
passages.summary: Judah will sing this song in that day. The singers have a strong city, and salvation is its walls. The LORD keeps a steady mind in peace because it trusts him. He brought the high city down, and the feet of the poor walk on it. The singers say they waited for the LORD through the night. Other lords ruled them, and their own efforts gave birth only to wind. Then comes a promise: “Your dead shall live.” The people are told to hide a little while until the anger passes.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The people say they “gave birth, it seems, only to wind” (verse 18). What does verse 19 promise next?

passages.title: A vineyard restored
passages.summary: In that day the LORD kills leviathan, the twisting serpent of the sea. In a new vineyard song, the LORD keeps the vineyard and waters it. He says he has no anger. Thorns may be burned or may make peace with him. Jacob will take root, and Israel will fill the world with fruit. Jacob’s sin is forgiven when the altar stones are crushed like chalk. The strong city lies empty. A great trumpet calls the lost from Assyria and Egypt to worship in Jerusalem.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The vineyard in chapter 5 gave wild grapes. What does Israel give in 27:6, and who waters it in verse 3?

passages.title: A foundation and false security
passages.summary: Woe comes to Ephraim’s drunk leaders, whose crown is a fading flower. A strong one from the Lord will throw it down like a hailstorm. Priests and prophets stagger with drink too. They ask if the teaching is for small children: “line on line, here a little.” Jerusalem’s rulers say they made a covenant with death. The Lord GOD lays a tested cornerstone in Zion and measures with justice. Hail will sweep away their shelter of lies. A farmer does not plow or thresh forever, and this wisdom comes from the LORD.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The rulers hide under a “covenant with death” (verse 15). What does the Lord GOD lay in Zion in verse 16?

passages.title: Jerusalem and hidden counsel
passages.summary: Woe comes to Ariel, the city where David camped. The LORD will camp against it, and its voice will whisper from the dust. Then its enemies blow away like chaff, like a dream after waking. The prophets are in a deep sleep, and the vision is like a sealed book. The Lord says this people honors him with lips while their hearts are far away. He will do a wonder, and the wisdom of the wise will fail. In a little while the deaf will hear and the blind will see. The humble will rejoice, and Jacob will no longer be ashamed.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: This people honors the Lord with their lips (verse 13). Where does the verse say their heart is?

passages.title: An alliance and an invitation
passages.summary: The LORD says woe to rebellious children who go to Egypt without asking him. Their envoys carry treasure through a desert, but Egypt’s help is empty. The people tell the prophets to say only pleasant things. So their sin is like a bulging wall that breaks at once. The Lord GOD offered rescue through returning and rest, and they refused. Still the LORD waits to be gracious. A voice will say, “This is the way.” He will heal his people and strike Assyria with his rod.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The Lord GOD says strength is “in quietness and in confidence” (verse 15). What did the people choose in verse 16?

studyNotes.title: Ann Madsen on hearing and following guidance
studyNotes.text: Ann N. Madsen is a Latter-day Saint Isaiah scholar. In an interview, she reads Isaiah 30:21 as an example of personal revelation. Her LDS application connects hearing God’s direction with following it.
studyNotes.application: Read verses 19–22 together. Guidance comes amid distress, and the people then reject their idols. In this passage, listening leads to a change in worship and conduct. Madsen’s personal application builds on this address to Judah.

passages.title: Horses cannot save
passages.summary: Woe comes to those who go down to Egypt for help. They trust many chariots and strong horsemen and do not seek the LORD. The Egyptians are men and not God, and their horses are flesh. When the LORD stretches out his hand, helper and helped fall together. The LORD will fight for Mount Zion like a lion over its prey. He will guard Jerusalem like hovering birds. Israel is called to return and throw away its idols. The Assyrian will fall by a sword that is not a man’s.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Judah trusts chariots “because they are many” (verse 1). What does verse 3 say horses are made of? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Justice and peace
passages.summary: A king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice. Each will be like shelter from wind and water in a dry place. Eyes will see, ears will listen, and fools will no longer be called noble. Then the speaker warns the women who feel safe. In little more than a year the grape harvest will fail. Thorns will grow, and the palace and city will be empty. This lasts until the Spirit is poured out from on high. Then justice lives in the land, and its fruit is peace and safe homes.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The women in verse 9 are “at ease.” How is the quietness in verse 17 different from theirs? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Help in a time of danger
passages.summary: Woe comes to a destroyer who has not yet been destroyed. The people ask the LORD to be gracious, because they have waited for him. Envoys of peace weep, the roads are empty, and the land withers. The LORD says, “Now I will arise.” Sinners in Zion ask who can live with the burning fire. The answer is one who walks rightly, refuses bribes, and turns from bloodshed. That person will see the king and a quiet Jerusalem. The LORD is judge, lawgiver, and king, and he will save.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Verse 22 calls the LORD judge, lawgiver, and king. What kind of person can live with him in verse 15? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: Judgment pictured through Edom
