passages.summary: All nations are called to listen. The LORD is angry with the nations and their armies. The sky rolls up like a scroll, and its stars fade like leaves. His sword comes down on Edom, with a great slaughter at Bozrah. The LORD has a day of vengeance for Zion’s cause. Edom’s streams turn to pitch, and its smoke rises forever. Owls, ravens, jackals, and snakes take over its palaces. The LORD’s book says not one of these animals will be missing.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD has “a year of recompense for the cause of Zion” (verse 8). Whose case is being settled? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question comes from the study guide. The lesson does not teach this chapter.

passages.title: A road home
passages.summary: The desert will be glad and bloom. It will see the glory of the LORD. Weak hands and shaking knees are to be made strong. The fearful are told that God will come and save them. Then the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, and the mute sing. Water breaks out in the dry land. A road called the Holy Way runs through it, and no lion is there. The LORD’s ransomed people come to Zion singing, and sorrow flees.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The ransomed walk a road with no lion on it (verses 9–10). What flees from them at the end of verse 10?

passages.title: The Assyrian crisis
passages.summary: In King Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, Sennacherib of Assyria captures Judah’s walled cities. He sends his officer Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem with a large army. Rabshakeh stops by the water channel of the upper pool. Three of Hezekiah’s officials come out to meet him. Assyrian palace reliefs also show Lachish.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · campaign setting
passages.uncertainty: The campaign took place in 701 BCE. The map connects the cities named in the passage. The exact route is unknown.

lds.text: Read Hezekiah’s crisis as an invitation to trust God while facing a real political danger. Church teaching treats the historical setting as the background for that spiritual question. Judah’s walled cities have fallen (verse 1). What is left for Hezekiah to trust?

studyNotes.title: See the Assyrian evidence
studyNotes.text: Isaiah 36:2 places the Assyrian mission at Lachish. A palace relief depicts Sennacherib receiving its spoils. The prism gives a royal account of the campaign. Open the footnotes to see both objects and their source summaries.

passages.title: A battle over trust
passages.summary: Rabshakeh asks what Hezekiah trusts. He calls Egypt a broken reed that cuts the hand that leans on it. He says the LORD himself sent Assyria. Judah’s officials ask for Aramaic, but he shouts in the Jews’ language. He offers the people food and a new land if they give up. He says no god has saved a land from Assyria. The people stay silent, as the king ordered.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · narrative setting
passages.uncertainty: Isaiah records these speeches as part of the account. No separate record from the campaign confirms their exact words.

lds.text: The repeated question of whom to trust can be read alongside Hezekiah’s leadership. Condie’s conference talk applies his example to communities choosing change. Rabshakeh asks what Hezekiah trusts (verse 4). Why do the people answer him with silence in verse 21?

passages.title: The letter and the prayer
passages.summary: Hezekiah tears his clothes, goes to the LORD’s house, and sends to Isaiah. Isaiah says not to fear: the king of Assyria will hear news and go home. Sennacherib sends a letter that mocks Hezekiah’s God. Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD. His prayer admits Assyria’s victories and says the fallen gods were wood and stone. He asks God to save Judah so all kingdoms know the LORD alone is God.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · narrative setting
passages.uncertainty: The passage explains the events through faith in God. It does not provide separate historical proof of how Jerusalem survived.

lds.text: Hezekiah’s prayer offers a faithful model for turning toward God in distress. This is a devotional reading of the narrative, alongside the evidence discussed in Historical mode. Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD (verse 14). What reason does verse 20 give for rescue?

studyNotes.title: Compare the accounts of Jerusalem
studyNotes.text: Isaiah credits God with saving Jerusalem. Sennacherib’s account emphasizes Judah’s losses and tribute. It does not claim Jerusalem’s capture. These sources do not establish the same explanation for the outcome.

passages.title: Jerusalem survives
passages.summary: Isaiah sends the LORD’s answer to Hezekiah. Zion laughs at Sennacherib, who has mocked the Holy One of Israel. The LORD says he planned Assyria’s victories long ago. He will turn Assyria back with a hook in its nose. A remnant of Judah will take root again. Isaiah’s account says the LORD’s angel struck 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh. Assyrian accounts describe a royal victory.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · main crisis
passages.uncertainty: The sources give different explanations. The app cannot confirm the exact battle route or the number of deaths.

lds.text: LDS teaching reads the city’s preservation as an expression of God’s power to deliver. The remnant image also invites reflection on renewal after devastation. Verse 31 promises a remnant that takes root. What does verse 35 say moves the LORD to defend the city?

passages.title: A later death closes the story
passages.summary: The chapter ends with Sennacherib’s death in his own land. His sons kill him in the house of his god Nisroch. His son Esar Haddon becomes king. Many years pass between his return home and his death.
passages.dateLabel: 681 BCE · later aftermath
passages.uncertainty: This verse describes a later time. Do not date it to the night or year of the 701 BCE crisis.

lds.text: A faithful reading sees the ending as fulfillment of the earlier prophecy. The timeline shows the years between these events. Sennacherib mocked Judah’s God and dies in his own god’s house (verse 38). What does that ending answer?

passages.title: Illness and a sign
passages.summary: Hezekiah is sick and near death. Isaiah tells him to set his house in order. Hezekiah turns to the wall, prays, and weeps. The LORD sends Isaiah back: he has heard, and he adds fifteen years. He also promises to defend the city from Assyria. As a sign, the shadow goes back ten steps on the sundial of Ahaz. Verse 6 shows why chapter order may differ from the order of events.
passages.dateLabel: Around the Assyrian crisis · date uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The map uses 701 BCE to show the setting. The date of Hezekiah’s illness is uncertain.

lds.text: The Lord’s promise to hear prayer offers hope in times of need. Hezekiah’s recovery does not promise the same outcome for every illness. Hezekiah turns to the wall and weeps (verses 2–3). What two things does verse 5 say the LORD has done?

passages.title: Hezekiah’s song after recovery
passages.summary: Hezekiah writes a poem after he recovers. He thought he would enter Sheol in the middle of his life. His life felt like a tent pulled down and cloth cut from a loom. He moaned like a dove and asked the Lord for help. Then he says God spoke, acted, and put his sins behind his back. Sheol cannot praise God, but the living can. Fathers will tell their children. Isaiah had told them to lay a cake of figs on the boil.
passages.dateLabel: Hezekiah’s lifetime · exact date unknown
passages.uncertainty: The poem appears in Isaiah 38, but its exact date is unknown. The map shows Jerusalem as its setting.

lds.text: Church teaching uses this passage to discuss suffering, mercy, and forgiveness. The poem offers ideas for reflection. It does not promise physical recovery for everyone. Hezekiah says the living can praise God (verse 19). What does he want fathers to tell children?

passages.title: Babylon and Judah’s future
passages.summary: The king of Babylon sends letters and a gift after Hezekiah’s sickness. Hezekiah is pleased and shows the envoys all his treasure and weapons. Isaiah asks where the men came from and what they saw. Hezekiah says they came from Babylon and saw everything. Isaiah gives the LORD’s word: all of it will be carried to Babylon. Some of Hezekiah’s own sons will serve in Babylon’s palace. Hezekiah calls the word good, because there will be peace in his days. McClellan compares this warning with Isaiah 40. Isaiah 40 speaks as if the exile has already happened. He uses this change to support a later date for Isaiah 40–55. Scholars often call this section Second Isaiah.
passages.dateLabel: Late eighth century BCE · embassy date debated
passages.uncertainty: The map uses 703 BCE to show the setting. The visit’s exact date is uncertain. Chapter order does not prove the visit followed the 701 BCE crisis. Select 597 or 587/586 BCE to study later events.

lds.text: The Church manual reads these chapters as a transition from Assyrian danger to Babylonian captivity. Consider the contrast between present security and responsibility for future generations. Hezekiah calls the word “good” because peace lasts his lifetime (verse 8). Who bears the cost in verse 7?

passages.title: Comfort and renewed strength
passages.summary: God says, “Comfort, comfort my people.” Jerusalem’s hard service is over, and her sin is pardoned. A voice calls for a level road in the desert for the LORD. Another voice says people are like grass, but God’s word stands forever. Zion is told to say, “Behold, your God!” He comes with power and carries lambs like a shepherd. No one taught him, and no nation or idol compares with him. Jacob says God has missed his case, yet those who wait gain new strength.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Jacob says, “My way is hidden from the LORD” (verse 27). How do verses 28–29 answer him?

passages.title: Do not fear
passages.summary: The LORD calls the far coasts to meet him in court. He asks who raised up a conqueror from the east. The answer is the LORD, the first and with the last. The nations are afraid, and their workers nail idols down so they will not fall. The LORD calls Israel his servant, chosen and not thrown away. He tells Israel not to fear, because he will help and hold it up. He will give water to the poor and trees to the desert. He dares the idols to tell the future, and they cannot.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The nations nail their idol so it will not fall (verse 7). Who holds whom up in verse 10?

passages.title: A servant who brings justice
passages.summary: The LORD presents his servant and puts his Spirit on him. The servant brings justice to the nations without shouting in the street. He does not break a bruised reed or put out a weak wick. He is a light for the nations, to open blind eyes and free prisoners. All the earth is called to sing a new song. The LORD, long silent, goes out like a warrior and leads the blind. Then he calls his own servant blind and deaf. Israel was robbed because it would not walk in his ways.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The servant will not break “a bruised reed” (verse 3). What is he sent to bring in verses 1 and 4?

passages.title: Called by name
passages.summary: The LORD who made Jacob says not to fear. He has redeemed Israel, called it by name, and says, “You are mine.” He will be with them through water and fire. He will gather their children from east, west, north, and south. The nations are called to court, and Israel is the LORD’s witness. For Israel’s sake he sends to Babylon. He is doing a new thing: a road and rivers in the desert. Israel wore him out with sins, yet he blots them out for his own sake.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD says, “You are mine” (verse 1). What does verse 2 promise in water and fire?

passages.title: The Creator and the idol maker
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jacob his servant not to fear. He will pour water on dry ground and his Spirit on their children. He is the first and the last, and there is no other God. Then the chapter describes an idol maker. He burns half a tree to cook and bows to the other half. No one stops to think that it is a block of wood. The LORD tells Israel he has wiped out its sins like a cloud. He says Jerusalem will be built, and he names Cyrus as his shepherd.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD calls Cyrus “my shepherd” (verse 28). What two things does the verse say will be built or laid?

passages.title: Cyrus and the LORD's purpose
passages.summary: The LORD speaks to Cyrus, his anointed, and holds his right hand. He will open gates before Cyrus and give him hidden treasure. He does this for Jacob’s sake, though Cyrus has not known him. The LORD says he forms light and darkness, peace and trouble. Woe comes to anyone who argues with his Maker, like clay with a potter. Cyrus will build the city and free the exiles without payment. The LORD did not speak in secret. He calls all the ends of the earth to look to him and be saved.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Cyrus has “not known” the LORD (verse 4). For whose sake does the verse say he is called?

passages.title: The God who carries
passages.summary: Bel and Nebo bow down. Animals carry their idols as heavy loads, and the idols go into captivity. The LORD tells Jacob’s house that he has carried them from birth. He will carry them to old age and gray hair. People pay a goldsmith to make a god, then lift it on their shoulders. It stands where they set it and cannot answer. The LORD declares the end from the beginning. He calls a bird of prey from the east and brings salvation to Zion.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: People carry their god on their shoulders (verse 7). Who carries whom in verse 4?

passages.title: Babylon brought down
passages.summary: Babylon is told to come down and sit in the dust. She will grind flour at the millstones and be called tender no more. The LORD says he gave his people into her hand, and she showed no mercy. She laid a heavy yoke even on the old. She said, “I will be a princess forever.” In one day she will lose both children and husband. Her spells and star readers cannot save her. They burn like stubble, and no one is left to help.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Babylon says, “No one sees me” (verse 10). What did she do to captives in verse 6?

passages.title: Leaving Babylon
passages.summary: The LORD speaks to Jacob’s house, who swear by his name but not in truth. He told them things long ago so they could not credit an idol. Now he tells new things they have not heard. He holds back his anger for his own name’s sake. He has tested them in the furnace of suffering. He says their peace would have been like a river if they had listened. Then the order comes: leave Babylon and shout that the LORD has redeemed Jacob. There is no peace for the wicked.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Israel is called stubborn in verse 4 and told to leave Babylon in verse 20. Why does the LORD act, according to verse 11?

passages.title: A servant and remembered Zion
passages.summary: The servant speaks to far peoples. The LORD called him before birth and made his mouth like a sharp sword. The servant says he has worked for nothing, yet his reward is with God. The LORD says restoring Israel is too small a task. The servant will be a light to the nations. Captives will come out and be led by springs of water. Zion says the LORD has forgotten her. He answers that a mother may forget her baby, but he will not forget Zion.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Zion says, “The LORD has forsaken me” (verse 14). What two pictures answer her in verses 15–16?

passages.title: A listening servant
passages.summary: The LORD asks for the divorce paper and the name of any lender he owed. He says the people were sold for their own sins. He asks why no one answered when he called. Then a servant speaks. The Lord GOD wakes his ear each morning and gives him words for the weary. He gave his back to those who beat him and did not hide from spitting. He sets his face like flint, because the Lord GOD will help him. Those who fear the LORD are told to trust him in the dark.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The servant’s ear is opened “morning by morning” (verse 4). What does he do with what he hears in verses 5–6?

passages.title: Remember and awaken
passages.summary: The LORD speaks to those who seek him. Look to Abraham and Sarah, he says: Abraham was one, and God made him many. The LORD will comfort Zion and make her desert like Eden. The sky will fade like smoke, but his salvation lasts forever. A voice calls the LORD’s arm to wake, as when it dried the sea. The LORD asks why they fear men who die like grass. Jerusalem has drunk the cup of his anger to the bottom. He takes the cup from her hand and gives it to those who hurt her.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD made Abraham many when he was “but one” (verse 2). What does verse 3 say he will do for Zion’s waste places?

passages.title: Good news for Zion
passages.summary: Zion is told to wake, put on fine clothes, and shake off the dust. The LORD says she was sold for nothing and will be bought back without money. His people were taken away, and his name is mocked all day. So they will know his name. A messenger runs on the mountains with good news: “Your God reigns!” The watchmen sing as the LORD returns to Zion. The people leave without rushing, with the LORD ahead and behind. The LORD says his marred servant will be lifted very high.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The messenger tells Zion that her God reigns (verse 7). Who was ruling over the people in verse 5?

passages.title: The suffering servant
passages.summary: A group speaks and asks who has believed their message. The servant grew like a root in dry ground, with no beauty to draw them. People despised him, and the speakers did not respect him. They thought God was striking him. But he carried their sickness and was pierced for their wrongs. Like a silent lamb, he did not open his mouth. He was cut off and buried with the wicked, though he had done no violence. After his suffering he will see light, and he will make many righteous.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The speakers first thought the servant was “struck by God” (verse 4). What do they say he carried?

passages.title: A covenant of peace
passages.summary: A woman with no children is told to sing. She will have many children, so she must make her tent bigger. She will forget the shame of her youth. Her Maker is her husband and her Redeemer. He left her for a short moment and gathers her with great mercy. As he swore about Noah’s flood, he swears not to be angry with her. He will rebuild her with jewels, and the LORD will teach her children. No weapon made against her will succeed.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Mountains may move, but two things will not leave (verse 10). What are they?

passages.title: An invitation without price
passages.summary: The LORD calls everyone who is thirsty to come to the water. Those with no money may buy wine and milk without price. He asks why they spend money on what is not bread. If they listen, they will live, and he will make a lasting covenant with them. They should seek the LORD while he is near and return for pardon. His thoughts are higher than theirs, as the sky is above the earth. His word is like rain: it does what he sends it to do. They will go out with joy, and the trees will clap.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD says to buy “without money and without price” (verse 1). What are people spending money on in verse 2?

passages.title: A house of prayer for all peoples
passages.summary: The LORD says to keep justice, because his salvation is near. The one who keeps the Sabbath and does no evil is blessed. A foreigner should not say the LORD will shut him out. A eunuch, a man who cannot father children, should not call himself a dry tree. The LORD will give faithful eunuchs a name better than sons and daughters. He will bring foreigners who hold to his covenant to his holy mountain. His house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples. But Israel’s watchmen are blind, like dogs that cannot bark.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: A foreigner fears the LORD will “separate me from his people” (verse 3). What does verse 7 promise instead?

passages.title: False worship and healing
passages.summary: Good people die, and no one thinks about it. They enter peace. Then the LORD charges others with worship under trees and killing children in the valleys. They set their bed on a high mountain and sent envoys far away. Their collected idols cannot save them, and a breath will carry them off. A voice says to clear the road for God’s people. The high and holy One says he also lives with the humble. He will not be angry forever and will heal, but the wicked have no peace.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The high and lofty One lives in two places (verse 15). What does he do for the humble there?

passages.title: The fast God chooses
passages.summary: The LORD tells the speaker to shout Israel’s sins like a trumpet. The people seek him daily and ask why he ignores their fasts. He answers that on fast days they push their workers and fight. Bowing the head like a reed is not the fast he chose. His fast is to free the oppressed and break every yoke. It is to feed the hungry, house the poor, and clothe the naked. Then their light will break out, and he will answer, “Here I am.” If they honor the Sabbath, they will delight in the LORD.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The people ask why God ignores their fast (verse 3). What fast does he choose in verses 6–7?

passages.title: Justice lost and a redeemer promised
passages.summary: The LORD’s hand is not too short to save, and his ear can hear. The people’s sins have come between them and God. Their hands shed blood, their lips lie, and no one goes to court honestly. Then the people speak: they look for light and walk in darkness. They admit that truth has fallen in the street. The LORD sees that there is no justice and no one to step in. So his own arm saves, and he puts on righteousness like armor. A Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from wrong.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD “wondered that there was no intercessor” (verse 16). What does he do when no one steps in?

passages.title: Zion receives light
passages.summary: Zion is told to rise and shine, because her light has come. Darkness covers the earth, but the LORD’s glory rises on her. Nations and kings come to her light. Her sons and daughters come home from far away. Camels bring gold and frankincense, and ships bring her children. Foreigners rebuild her walls, and her gates stay open day and night. Peace and righteousness will rule her, and violence will end. The LORD will be her lasting light in place of sun and moon.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Nations come to Zion’s light (verse 3). Whose light does verse 1 say it is?

passages.title: Good news and restored lives
passages.summary: A speaker says the Lord GOD’s Spirit is on him. The LORD has anointed him to bring good news to the humble. He is sent to heal broken hearts and announce freedom to captives. He proclaims the year of the LORD’s favor and comforts those who mourn. They get a garland in place of ashes and will rebuild old ruins. They will be called the LORD’s priests. The LORD says he loves justice and will make a lasting covenant with them. The speaker rejoices, clothed in salvation like a bride or groom.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The speaker is sent to “proclaim liberty to the captives” (verse 1). What do the freed people do in verse 4?

passages.title: A new name for Zion
passages.summary: The speaker will not keep quiet until Zion’s righteousness shines like dawn. Nations and kings will see it, and the LORD will give her a new name. She will no longer be called Forsaken, or her land Desolate. Her new names are Hephzibah and Beulah, because the LORD delights in her. God will rejoice over her as a groom over a bride. Watchmen on the walls must give the LORD no rest. He swears that enemies will no longer eat her grain. The people will be called the Holy People, the LORD’s Redeemed.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Zion called herself forsaken in 49:14. What two new names does she get in 62:4, and why?

passages.title: Judgment and remembered mercy
passages.summary: A watcher asks who comes from Edom in red clothes. The one coming says he trod the wine press alone, in anger, with no helper. Then a speaker recalls the LORD’s loving kindness to Israel. He became their Savior and carried them in the old days. But they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, and he fought against them. The people remember Moses and the sea. They ask God to look down, calling him “our Father.” They ask why enemies have trampled his holy place.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Verse 9 says, “In all their affliction he was afflicted.” What did the people do next in verse 10?

passages.title: A prayer for God's return
passages.summary: The prayer goes on. The people ask God to tear the heavens and come down, as he once did. No eye has seen a God like him, who works for those who wait. They confess long sin and ask, “Shall we be saved?” All their right acts are like a dirty cloth, and they fade like leaves. No one calls on his name. Still they call him Father and potter, and themselves clay. Zion is a wilderness, the temple is burned, and they ask for an answer.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The people call their right acts “a polluted garment” (verse 6). What do they call God in verse 8?

passages.title: Judgment and new creation
passages.summary: The LORD says he let himself be found by people who did not seek him. All day he held out his hands to a rebellious people. They offer sacrifices in gardens, sit among graves, and eat pig’s meat. He will repay them, yet he spares some, like a good grape cluster. His servants will eat and sing, and those who left him will go hungry. Then he says he creates new heavens and a new earth. People will build houses and live in them, and plant vineyards and eat. Wolf and lamb will feed together.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: In the new earth, people “will not build and another inhabit” (verse 22). What loss from chapter 1 does that undo?

passages.title: Humility, comfort, and all nations
passages.summary: The LORD says heaven is his throne and earth his footstool. He asks what house people could build for him. He looks to the one who is poor, sorry, and trembles at his word. He rejects offerings from those who choose their own ways. Zion gives birth to a nation in one day, before her pain comes. The LORD will comfort Jerusalem as a mother comforts her child. He comes with fire to judge, and gathers all nations to see his glory. All flesh will worship him, and the rebels’ bodies lie outside.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: The LORD asks what house anyone could build for him (verse 1). To whom does he look in verse 2?

events.title: Early eighth-century setting
events.summary: Judah and Israel face the growing power of Assyria. This date shows an earlier setting. It does not mark one event.
events.uncertainty: 780 BCE is where the timeline starts. It is not Isaiah’s birth or a campaign.

events.title: The northern kingdom falls
events.summary: Rabshakeh uses Samaria’s fall as a warning in Isaiah 36:19. Assyria took the city, faced another revolt, and tightened its control.
events.uncertainty: 722/721 BCE covers several steps of conquest and control. Scholars differ on the date of each step.

events.title: A new Assyrian king
events.summary: Sargon II dies, and Sennacherib becomes king of Assyria. Lands under Assyria push back against its rule.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Babylon challenges Assyria
events.summary: Sennacherib defeats Merodach-baladan in Babylonia. Isaiah 39:1 names this ruler. He sends letters and a gift to Hezekiah.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Sennacherib’s western campaign
events.summary: The Assyrian army reaches Judah. Isaiah, the royal Assyrian writings, and the Lachish wall carvings each tell of it.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Palace reliefs show Lachish
events.summary: The palace wall carvings show the fall of Lachish for the Assyrian court. Carvers made them after the event.
events.uncertainty: The museum dates the reliefs to 700–692 BCE. The timeline shows them at 695 BCE.

events.title: Sennacherib’s reign ends
events.summary: Isaiah 37:38 tells of Sennacherib’s death. His sons kill him many years after the invasion.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Nineveh falls
events.summary: Nineveh falls, and Assyria grows weak. Some Assyrian forces keep fighting.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Babylon gains power in the west
events.summary: The battle at Carchemish helps Babylon gain power in the eastern Mediterranean region.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Jerusalem and royal deportation
events.summary: Babylon captures Jerusalem and takes its king into exile. These later events help explain the warning in Isaiah 39.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Jerusalem and the temple destroyed
events.summary: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple. This happens long after the Assyrian crisis.
events.uncertainty: Scholars date the destruction to 587 or 586 BCE. The app shows both dates.

events.title: Persia takes Babylon
events.summary: Cyrus conquers Babylon. The Cyrus Cylinder says he helped restore worship. It does not mention the return of Judah’s exiles.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.summary: Jerusalem was Judah’s capital and the home of its royal court and temple. Its ridge-top position made it defensible but not isolated.
places.detail: Jerusalem is the political and spiritual center of Isaiah’s world. Assyrian pressure, royal policy, temple worship, judgment, and hope all meet here.

places.name: Lachish
places.summary: Lachish was a major fortified city southwest of Jerusalem. It guarded roads through Judah’s western lowlands.
places.detail: Assyria’s capture of Lachish exposed Jerusalem to direct attack. Its fall shows how much of Judah was lost even though the capital survived.

places.name: Nineveh
places.summary: Nineveh became Sennacherib’s royal capital on the Tigris. Its palaces displayed Assyrian wealth, building, and military victories.
places.detail: Nineveh represents the imperial power that threatened Judah. It also preserves Assyrian art and inscriptions that can be compared with Isaiah’s account.

places.name: Babylon
places.summary: Babylon was a major city on the Euphrates and a center of southern Mesopotamian power. Its kings often competed with Assyria before Babylon became an empire.
places.detail: In Isaiah, Babylon first appears as a rival under Assyrian rule. It later becomes the power linked with Judah’s exile. It then becomes the place where a promised return begins.

places.name: Samaria
places.summary: Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel. Assyria captured it and deported part of its population.
places.detail: Samaria’s fall showed Judah what Assyrian conquest could do to a neighboring kingdom. Isaiah treats that disaster as both a warning and part of the region’s political upheaval.

places.name: Hamath
places.summary: Hamath was an important kingdom and city on the Orontes in western Syria. It stood on routes between inland Syria and the Mediterranean coast.
places.detail: Assyria’s defeat of Hamath made it a warning to other western kingdoms. Isaiah uses such fallen cities to expose the empire’s argument that resistance is useless.

places.name: Arpad
places.summary: Arpad was a north Syrian city-state near Aleppo. Assyria fought repeated campaigns there before making it part of the empire.
places.detail: Arpad’s long resistance ended in Assyrian conquest. Its defeat became part of Assyria’s political message to cities such as Jerusalem.

places.name: Harran
places.summary: Harran was a trading and religious center on routes across northern Mesopotamia. Its position linked Assyria, Syria, and Anatolia.
places.detail: Harran shows the reach of Assyrian control far beyond Judah. Isaiah includes conquered northern cities in the empire’s attempt to intimidate Jerusalem.

places.name: Gozan
places.summary: Gozan is usually linked with Guzana at Tell Halaf. It became an Assyrian provincial center in northern Mesopotamia.
places.detail: Gozan became part of the Assyrian system of provinces and deportation. Its name helps Isaiah’s readers feel the scale of Assyria’s earlier conquests.

places.name: Libnah
places.summary: Libnah was a fortified town in Judah’s western lowlands. Its exact site remains uncertain.
places.uncertainty: This is a representative location. Competing site identifications exist; the coordinate does not settle them.
places.detail: Libnah matters because the Assyrian campaign did not stop at Lachish. Its uncertain location also warns against drawing a precise military route from the text.

places.name: Tyre
places.summary: Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port with an island center. Its merchants connected the Levant with Mediterranean trade.
places.detail: Isaiah uses Phoenician trade to make a clear point. Wealth and wide influence cannot keep a city safe. These ports also show Judah in a larger trade world.

places.name: Sidon
places.summary: Sidon was a major Phoenician port north of Tyre. Its ships and workshops formed part of a wide Mediterranean trade network.
places.detail: Isaiah uses Phoenician trade to make a clear point. Wealth and wide influence cannot keep a city safe. These ports also show Judah in a larger trade world.

places.name: Ashkelon
places.summary: Ashkelon was a fortified Philistine port on the southern coast. Trade routes and armies passed through its region.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Ekron
places.summary: Ekron was a large Philistine city with strong olive-oil production. Its rulers balanced local interests against Assyrian demands.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Memphis · Egypt
places.summary: Memphis was a major city near the head of the Nile Delta. It was a political and religious center of Egypt.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Damascus
places.summary: Damascus was the capital of Aram-Damascus and an important inland trade center. It controlled routes through southern Syria.
places.detail: Damascus joined Israel against Judah before it fell to Assyria. Its rise and defeat show how small kingdoms formed coalitions under imperial pressure.

places.name: Carchemish
places.summary: Carchemish was a fortified city at a major Euphrates crossing. Armies and trade routes moved through this strategic point.
places.detail: Babylon later won a battle at Carchemish. This victory moved control of Syria and the Levant away from Egypt. That change helps explain the Babylonian future in Isaiah.

places.name: Susa
places.summary: Susa was an ancient city east of Babylon and later a Persian royal center. It linked Mesopotamia with the Iranian plateau.
places.detail: Susa belongs to the Persian horizon that follows Babylon. Persia’s rise provides the political setting for Isaiah’s promises connected with Cyrus.

places.name: Aiath
places.summary: Aiath was a town north of Jerusalem. Its exact identification remains debated.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Anathoth
places.summary: Anathoth was a small town a few miles northeast of Jerusalem. It belonged to the territory of Benjamin.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Ar
places.summary: Ar was an important settlement in Moab. Its exact site is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Arnon
places.summary: The Arnon is the deep gorge now called Wadi Mujib. It cut across Moab and formed a major natural boundary.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Aroer
places.summary: Aroer was a settlement east of the Jordan. More than one ancient place used this name.
places.detail: Aroer helps locate the borderlands east of Israel. Isaiah uses abandoned towns there to show the reach of regional collapse.

places.name: Ashdod
places.summary: Ashdod was a fortified Philistine city near the Mediterranean coast. It controlled rich farmland and access to coastal trade.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Assyria
places.summary: Assyria was an empire centered in northern Mesopotamia. Its armies, governors, tribute system, and deportations reshaped the Levant.
places.detail: Assyria is the main political power in much of Isaiah 1–39. The book presents Assyria as a human empire. It also shows God using Assyria and judging its violence and pride.

places.name: Bashan
places.summary: Bashan was a fertile upland east of the Sea of Galilee. It was known for forests, pasture, and strong cattle.
places.detail: Bashan’s famous strength and fertility make it a useful image of human grandeur. Isaiah places such grandeur under God’s judgment.

places.name: Beer-elim
places.summary: Beer-elim was a Moabite location known from the biblical text. Its exact site is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Bozrah
places.summary: Bozrah was a chief city of Edom in the highlands southeast of Judah. It stood near routes through the Arabah and Transjordan.
places.detail: Edom was Judah’s neighbor and frequent rival. Isaiah uses its land to speak about regional judgment and the reversal of power.

places.name: Calneh
places.summary: Calneh was a north Syrian city associated with the region of Arpad. Its exact identification is debated.
places.detail: Calneh belongs to the list of cities Assyria claimed to have overcome. The comparison turns geography into imperial propaganda aimed at Jerusalem.

places.name: Cush
places.summary: Cush was the kingdom south of Egypt, centered in Nubia. Cushite rulers also governed Egypt during part of Isaiah’s lifetime.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Cyprus
places.summary: Cyprus was a large Mediterranean island with ports, copper resources, and wide trade links. Biblical Kittim often points toward Cyprus and the western sea.
places.detail: Isaiah uses Phoenician trade to make a clear point. Wealth and wide influence cannot keep a city safe. These ports also show Judah in a larger trade world.

places.name: Dedan
places.summary: Dedan was an oasis and caravan center in northwestern Arabia. Traders carried incense and other goods through this region.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Dibon
places.summary: Dibon was a prominent Moabite city east of the Dead Sea. It stood near the King’s Highway and controlled nearby farmland.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Edom
places.summary: Edom occupied the highlands south and southeast of the Dead Sea. Its territory controlled routes between Judah, Arabia, and the Red Sea.
places.detail: Edom was Judah’s neighbor and frequent rival. Isaiah uses its land to speak about regional judgment and the reversal of power.

places.name: Egypt
places.summary: Egypt was an old kingdom centered on the Nile. Its wealth and armies made it a possible ally and a rival great power.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Elam
places.summary: Elam was a kingdom east of Babylonia in southwestern Iran. It sometimes allied with Babylon against Assyria.
places.detail: This place helps show how Isaiah’s world connected small kingdoms, trade routes, and competing empires.

places.name: Elealeh
places.summary: Elealeh was a Moabite town on the plateau east of the Dead Sea. It lay close to Heshbon.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Euphrates
places.summary: The Euphrates was the great river running from Anatolia through Syria and Mesopotamia. Major cities and imperial routes followed its valley.
places.detail: The Euphrates often marks the direction from which Mesopotamian empires reached Syria and Judah. Isaiah uses its floodwaters as an image of Assyria’s overwhelming advance.

places.name: Galilee
places.summary: Galilee was the northern region around the Sea of Galilee. It lay near international roads and was exposed to invasion from the north.
places.detail: Galilee was among the first Israelite regions to suffer Assyrian conquest. Isaiah turns this exposed borderland into a setting for renewed hope.

places.name: Geba
places.summary: Geba was a Benjaminite town north of Jerusalem. It stood near a pass through the central hill country.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Gibeah
places.summary: Gibeah was a Benjaminite hill town just north of Jerusalem. Its elevated position overlooked approaches to the capital.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Hanes
places.summary: Hanes was an Egyptian center, probably in the Nile Valley. Its exact role and identification in this period remain uncertain.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Heshbon
places.summary: Heshbon was a major town on the plateau east of the Jordan. It sat near roads linking Ammon, Moab, and the north.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Horonaim
places.summary: Horonaim was a Moabite town, probably near a descent toward the Dead Sea. Its exact location remains uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Jahaz
places.summary: Jahaz was a settlement on the Moabite plateau. Its precise site remains debated.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Jazer
places.summary: Jazer was a town east of the Jordan near productive fields and vineyards. Its exact site is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Kedar
places.summary: Kedar was a confederation of Arabian pastoral and trading groups. Its people moved across routes east and south of the Levant.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Kir-hareseth
places.summary: Kir-hareseth was a major fortified center in Moab, often linked with modern Kerak. It stood above routes south of the Arnon.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Lebanon
places.summary: Lebanon was the mountain region north of Israel, famous for cedar forests. Its timber and passes had economic and strategic value.
places.detail: Isaiah uses Lebanon’s cedars as images of wealth, height, and royal power. Their fall represents the humbling of proud rulers and empires.

places.name: Luhith
places.summary: Luhith was a Moabite site associated with an uphill road. Its precise location is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Medeba
places.summary: Medeba was a town on the Moabite plateau east of the Dead Sea. Its surrounding plain supported farming and travel.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Media
places.summary: Media was a kingdom on the Iranian plateau east of Assyria. Median forces later helped Babylon defeat the Assyrian Empire.
places.detail: The Medes helped end Assyrian rule and later became part of the Persian imperial world. Their appearance marks how quickly the balance of power could change.

places.name: Michmash
places.summary: Michmash was a hill town north of Jerusalem near a narrow pass. The pass made it important for travel and defense.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Midian
places.summary: Midian was a broad region south and east of the Gulf of Aqaba. The name also described groups of people. Its routes connected Arabia with the Levant.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Migron
places.summary: Migron was a site north of Jerusalem near Michmash. Its precise identification is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Moab
places.summary: Moab occupied the plateau east of the Dead Sea. Its towns, farms, and roads lay between Judah, Ammon, Edom, and Arabia.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Mount Carmel
places.summary: Mount Carmel is a wooded ridge reaching the Mediterranean coast. It overlooks the coastal plain and the Jezreel Valley.
places.detail: Carmel’s fertility made its withering a strong image of national disaster. Its recovery could also signal renewed life.

places.name: Mount Seir
places.summary: Mount Seir was the rugged highland associated with Edom. Its ridges controlled routes through the southern Transjordan.
places.detail: Edom was Judah’s neighbor and frequent rival. Isaiah uses its land to speak about regional judgment and the reversal of power.

places.name: Nebo
places.summary: Nebo was a Moabite town east of the Dead Sea. It was also a center for worship. Its exact ancient site is usually placed near Mount Nebo.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Negeb
places.summary: The Negeb was Judah’s dry southern region. Roads through it linked the hill country with Egypt, Edom, and Arabia.
places.detail: The Negeb was a route for messengers, gifts, and armies moving toward Egypt. Isaiah uses it when criticizing Judah’s search for Egyptian protection.

places.name: Nile
places.summary: The Nile sustained Egypt’s farms, cities, and transport. Control of its water and harvests supported Egyptian power.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Nimrim
places.summary: Nimrim was a place with much water in Moab. It is often linked with a stream south of the Dead Sea. Its exact identification is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Nob
places.summary: Nob was a settlement close to Jerusalem, probably on a northern approach. Its exact location remains uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Pathros
places.summary: Pathros means Upper Egypt, the Nile Valley south of the Delta. It was one of Egypt’s main historic regions.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Philistia
places.summary: Philistia was the coastal plain ruled by cities such as Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron. Its ports and roads made it valuable to larger empires.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Ramah
places.summary: Ramah was a Benjaminite town north of Jerusalem. It stood along an important ridge route.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Rezeph
places.summary: Rezeph was a fortified city on routes across the Syrian desert. It later became an Assyrian provincial center.
places.detail: Rezeph was another city taken by Assyria. Its fate supports Assyria’s proud claim. Assyria says that no local god or king could resist its power.

places.name: Sela
places.summary: Sela means rock and probably points to a stronghold in the Edomite highlands. Its exact identification is debated.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Sharon
places.summary: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain west of the central hills. Its fields and north-south road gave it economic value.
places.detail: Sharon links the coast with Judah’s hill country. Isaiah uses its fertile landscape to measure both devastation and restoration.

places.name: Sheba
places.summary: Sheba was a wealthy south Arabian kingdom linked with incense and caravan trade. Its merchants connected Arabia with the Levant.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Sibmah
places.summary: Sibmah was a Moabite town known for vineyards. Its exact location near Heshbon is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Tema
places.summary: Tema was a major oasis in northern Arabia. It served caravans moving between Arabia, Mesopotamia, and the Levant.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Valley of Achor
places.summary: The Valley of Achor lay near the approaches to Jericho. Its exact extent is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah turns this remembered place of trouble into pasture for a restored people. The geography supports the movement from judgment to hope.

places.name: Zoan
places.summary: Zoan, or Tanis, was an important city in the eastern Nile Delta. It was close to routes between Egypt and the Levant.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Zoar
places.summary: Zoar was a town near the southern end of the Dead Sea. Its exact site is debated.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Brook of the Willows
places.summary: The Brook of the Willows was a stream or wadi on Moab’s border. It is often linked with Wadi al-Hasa.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Eglaim
places.summary: Eglaim was a Moabite location known from the biblical text. Its exact site is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Eglath-shelishiyah
places.summary: Eglath-shelishiyah was a place near the southern Dead Sea. Its exact identification is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Javan
places.summary: Javan is the biblical name for Ionia and, more broadly, Greek lands across the sea. It represents the western Mediterranean world.
places.detail: These distant peoples widen Isaiah’s horizon beyond Judah and its immediate enemies. They help frame the book’s final vision as international in scope.

places.name: Lud
places.summary: Lud probably points to Lydia in western Anatolia. It represents a distant people beyond the eastern Mediterranean.
places.detail: These distant peoples widen Isaiah’s horizon beyond Judah and its immediate enemies. They help frame the book’s final vision as international in scope.

places.name: Tubal
places.summary: Tubal was a people and kingdom in Anatolia. Assyrian records place it north of Syria in the mountain lands.
places.detail: These distant peoples widen Isaiah’s horizon beyond Judah and its immediate enemies. They help frame the book’s final vision as international in scope.

places.name: Joppa / Jaffa
places.summary: Joppa, now Jaffa, was a port on the central coast. It connected inland towns with Mediterranean shipping.
places.uncertainty: Representative site coordinates, not the position of an ancient road.
places.detail: Isaiah uses Phoenician trade to make a clear point. Wealth and wide influence cannot keep a city safe. These ports also show Judah in a larger trade world.

places.name: Timnah · Tel Batash
places.summary: Timnah was a Philistine-border town in the Sorek Valley. Its farmland and road position made it a contested place.
places.uncertainty: Representative site coordinates, not the position of an ancient road.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Azekah
places.summary: Azekah was a fortified town above the Elah Valley. It guarded routes from the coastal plain into Judah’s hills.
places.uncertainty: Representative site coordinates, not the position of an ancient road.
places.detail: This place helps show how Isaiah’s world connected small kingdoms, trade routes, and competing empires.

campaigns.title: From Lachish to Jerusalem
campaigns.summary: In Isaiah 36:2, the king of Assyria sends Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem. He comes with a large army.
campaigns.detail: Isaiah does not name Rabshakeh’s road. The line does not show where Sennacherib himself went. Assyrian palace reliefs also show Lachish.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects places in the account. The exact route is unknown.

campaigns.evidence: Named sites · travel order not established
campaigns.uncertainty: Lines connect sites affected by the campaign. They do not trace roads or establish travel order.
campaigns.title: The campaign along the coast
campaigns.summary: The Assyrian account describes the surrender of Phoenician centers. It also describes attacks on southern coastal towns.
campaigns.detail: Joppa is a named place in the annals. Ancient Tyre had island and mainland settlements. The line does not claim that Assyria captured the island city. The map order is not a confirmed march order.

campaigns.title: The Babylonian embassy
campaigns.dateLabel: Late eighth century BCE · exact date debated
campaigns.summary: In Isaiah 39, Babylon’s king sends envoys to Hezekiah with letters and a gift.
campaigns.detail: The line links the embassy’s origin and destination. Isaiah 39 does not name intermediate stops or establish the visit’s exact year.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects the two cities. The travel route and exact date are unknown.

campaigns.title: Exile in Babylon
campaigns.summary: Isaiah 39:6–7 gives a warning. The king’s treasures and some of his sons will go to Babylon. Babylon later took Jerusalem’s king into exile.
campaigns.detail: No one road into exile is known. People did not travel the whole time from 597 to 539 BCE.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects the cities. The exact route into exile is unknown.

campaigns.evidence: Named sites · travel order not established
campaigns.uncertainty: Lines connect sites affected by the campaign. They do not trace roads or establish travel order.
campaigns.title: Timnah and Ekron
campaigns.summary: The annals name the capture of Eltekeh and Timnah. They then describe action at Ekron.
campaigns.detail: The map connects the known sites of Timnah and Ekron. Experts do not agree about Eltekeh’s location. The explanation includes the battle, but the map has no exact point. The order in a royal account does not show the road.

campaigns.evidence: Named sites · travel order not established
campaigns.uncertainty: Lines connect sites affected by the campaign. They do not trace roads or establish travel order.
campaigns.title: Fortified towns of Judah
campaigns.summary: Azekah and Lachish help place attacks on Judah’s walled towns. Both cities were in the lowlands.
campaigns.detail: The Azekah writing and the evidence at Lachish describe separate attacks. They do not show which attack came first. This line shows the regional setting of Isaiah 36:1. It does not show a confirmed march between the attacks.

regions.name: Land near Babylon · approximate
regions.summary: Babylonia occupied the river plain of southern Mesopotamia, with Babylon as its leading city. Its rulers controlled rich farmland, temples, and trade routes but often faced Assyrian intervention.
regions.uncertainty: The shape does not show a firm border. Rule changed over time. Sennacherib beat Merodach-baladan in 703 BCE. Babylon became the main power in 605 BCE.
regions.detail: Babylon mattered to Isaiah before it became the next great empire. Merodach-baladan challenged Assyria and contacted Hezekiah. Babylon could seem like a possible ally. It also warned of Judah’s future.

regions.name: Land of Judah · approximate
regions.summary: Judah was a small hill kingdom centered on Jerusalem. Its farms, walled towns, and roads supported the capital. They connected it with the coast, Jordan Valley, and south.
regions.uncertainty: The shape does not show a firm border. Rule changed over time.
regions.detail: Judah stood between larger powers and had to choose between revolt, tribute, and foreign alliances. Isaiah addresses those choices while warning that political plans cannot replace faithful leadership.

regions.name: Philistine city-states · approximate
regions.summary: Philistia had several city-states on the southern coast. They included Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, Gaza, and Gath. The cities could work together, compete, or answer to a larger empire.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Control changed by city and year. Assyria and Babylon both put pressure on these cities.
regions.detail: Philistia matters because its cities stood on a major coastal route. The route joined Egypt with the Levant. Its rulers appear in warnings, revolts, alliances, and the campaign against Judah.

regions.name: Egyptian realm · approximate
regions.summary: Egypt controlled the Nile valley and delta. Egypt had divided rulers, armies, horses, and wealth. Judah saw it as a strong but unsafe ally.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Egypt’s ruling families and power centers changed during Isaiah’s time. Kushite rulers also governed Egypt for part of this period.
regions.detail: Isaiah presents Egypt as a major nation in God’s wider plans. He also warns Judah not to put its trust in Egypt. Chapters 30–31 challenge Judah’s trust in Egyptian horses and military help.

regions.name: Cushite realm · approximate
regions.summary: Cush was a kingdom south of Egypt in Nubia. Kushite kings also ruled Egypt as its Twenty-fifth Dynasty during part of Isaiah’s historical setting.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It shows only the northern part of Cush. Control changed over time.
regions.detail: Cush appears in Isaiah as a distant nation. Its messengers travel north. It also joins the conflict between Egypt and Assyria. Isaiah 37 names Tirhakah, usually identified with the Kushite ruler Taharqa.

regions.name: Lands under Assyria · approximate
regions.summary: The Neo-Assyrian Empire expanded from northern Mesopotamia to the Mediterranean and Egypt. It ruled through armies, governors, tribute, local client kings, and forced population movement.
regions.uncertainty: Assyria did not rule all these lands in the same way. Its power also changed over time. The shape does not show a firm border for each year.
regions.detail: Assyria caused the main political crisis in much of Isaiah 1–39. Assyria destroyed Israel and caused great harm in Judah. Jerusalem then had to decide where to place its trust.

regions.name: Lands under Babylon · approximate
regions.summary: The Neo-Babylonian Empire replaced Assyria as the main power in Mesopotamia and the Levant. Under Nebuchadnezzar II, Babylon conquered Jerusalem and deported many Judeans.
regions.uncertainty: The shape does not show a firm border. Rule changed over time.
regions.detail: Babylon is central to Isaiah’s words about exile and return. Babylon is the power that carries Judah away. It is also the empire that the exiles must later leave.

regions.name: Lands under Persia · approximate
regions.summary: Cyrus and the Persian Empire took Babylon in 539 BCE. Persia then joined Babylon’s lands to a much larger kingdom. Persian kings often governed through existing local leaders and offices.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows only part of the land Cyrus ruled.
regions.detail: Persia matters because Cyrus’s rise changed the future of displaced Judeans. Isaiah presents him as the ruler who makes Jerusalem’s restoration politically possible.

words.label: King
words.meaning: A ruler. The verse names both Judah’s king and the Assyrian king.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H4428. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Both men have the title king, but they are not equal. In verse 4, Rabshakeh calls his master “the great king.”

words.label: Hezekiah
words.meaning: The king of Judah in this account.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H2396. The verse may use another form.

words.label: Sennacherib
words.meaning: The king of Assyria. In verse 1, he attacks the fortified cities of Judah.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H5576. The verse may use another form.

words.label: Assyria
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H804. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The Hebrew names the land, Assyria. The Greek phrase names the people: king of the Assyrians.

words.label: Judah
words.meaning: The southern kingdom in this passage.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H3063. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Judah can also name an ancestor, a people, or a land. Here it has fortified cities, so it means the kingdom.

words.label: Rabshakeh
words.meaning: An Assyrian official’s title. The translation uses an English spelling of its sounds.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H7262. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Strong’s Hebrew dictionary explains Rabshakeh as “chief cupbearer.” This official served drinks to the king. In Isaiah 36, he speaks for the Assyrian king. He urges Jerusalem to surrender.

words.label: Lachish
words.meaning: A fortified city of Judah. The Assyrian king sends Rabshakeh from there to Jerusalem.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H3923. The verse may use another form.

words.label: Jerusalem
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H3389. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 36:2, the Hebrew word has an ending that means toward Jerusalem. English shows this direction with the separate word “to.”

words.label: Army
words.meaning: A force of soldiers in this verse.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H2426. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The Hebrew word can mean force or strength. Here it means the soldiers the king sends. The Greek word can also mean power or force.

words.label: Aqueduct
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H8585. The verse may use another form.

words.label: Pool
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H1295. The verse may use another form.

words.label: Confidence
words.greekNote: Swete’s text uses πεποιθὼς in verse 4. This verb form expresses trust in a question. It is not a noun like “confidence.”
words.meaning: Something a person relies on. Rabshakeh asks what Hezekiah relies on.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H986. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Isaiah 36:4 uses the Hebrew noun for confidence. The same question uses the related verb for trust. The pair opens the main question: whom can Judah trust?

words.label: Trust
words.greekNote: This form comes from verse 5. The Greek verb has different forms elsewhere in the chapter.
words.meaning: To rely on someone or something.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H982. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Rabshakeh attacks trust in Egypt’s army in Isaiah 36:6 and 9. He attacks trust in the LORD’s rescue in verse 15. His speech attacks both reasons for resisting Assyria.

words.label: Egypt
words.meaning: The country to the southwest of Judah. Rabshakeh says Judah trusts it for help.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H4714. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Rabshakeh calls Egypt a bruised reed. He says it will pierce the hand of a man who leans on it.

words.label: Aramaic
words.greekNote: The Greek word Συριστί names the language. It does not refer to a modern country.
words.meaning: The language Hezekiah’s officials ask Rabshakeh to speak.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H762. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The officials understand Aramaic. They do not want the people on the wall to hear. Rabshakeh keeps speaking in the Jews’ language.

words.label: Jews’ language
words.meaning: In Judean, the language the people on the wall speak. This translation says “the Jews’ language.”
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H3066. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: One Hebrew word matches the English phrase “the Jews’ language.” In Isaiah 36:13, Rabshakeh speaks directly to the people on the wall.

words.label: Remnant
words.greekNote: This Greek form comes from verse 4 and means those left. Verse 32 uses another form. Verse 31 uses different Hebrew wording, so this note does not cover it.
words.meaning: The people who remain after a disaster or loss.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H7611. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 37:4, Hezekiah asks for prayer for the survivors. In verses 31–32, they take root again and bear fruit. The picture shows survivors who start to grow again.

words.label: Spirit
words.meaning: A spirit or state of mind. God says he will put it in the Assyrian king.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H7307. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The Hebrew word can mean wind, breath, or spirit. In Isaiah 37:7, the Assyrian king then hears news and returns home.

words.label: Shadow
words.meaning: A shadow. As a sign for Hezekiah, God makes it return ten steps.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H6738. The verse may use another form.

words.label: Steps / sundial
words.meaning: Steps or degrees. Some translations use “sundial” for the structure where the shadow appears.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H4609. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The World English Bible says “sundial” where the Hebrew speaks of steps. The Hebrew does not describe a round clock face.

words.label: Sheol
words.meaning: The place of the dead in Hezekiah’s poem.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H7585. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Isaiah 38:18–19 contrasts the dead with the living. The dead cannot praise God, but the living can. Hezekiah gives praise after God saves him from death.

related.label: Matthew 16:18 — gates of Hades
related.note: A later verse with a similar picture. This note does not claim that Matthew quotes Isaiah 38.

words.label: Soul / life
words.meaning: Hezekiah’s life or self. God delivers it from the pit.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H5315. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Isaiah 38:17 names two acts of God. He saves Hezekiah’s life. He also casts Hezekiah’s sins behind his back.

words.label: Sins
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H2399. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 38:17, God casts Hezekiah’s sins behind his back. This picture expresses forgiveness. The same verse thanks God for saving Hezekiah’s life.

words.label: Babylon
words.greekNote: This form comes from verse 1. Later verses use other word forms and names for the people.
words.meaning: The city and kingdom of the visitors. Isaiah also names Babylon in his warning about the future.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H894. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Babylon sends a gift in Isaiah 39:1. In verse 6, Judah’s lost treasures will go to Babylon. The warning concerns the same wealth Hezekiah showed the visitors.

words.label: Eunuchs
words.meaning: Servants in a king’s court. The word can mean eunuchs or officials.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H5631. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 39:7, Hezekiah’s descendants serve in the Babylonian king’s palace. Sons of Judah’s royal family will serve a foreign king.

words.label: Peace
words.meaning: Peace or well-being in Hezekiah’s days.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H7965. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Isaiah 39:8 says that Hezekiah expects peace in his own days. He says this after hearing that his descendants will be taken away. His answer sets safety now beside the loss Isaiah says will come.

words.label: Truth / stability
words.greekNote: Swete’s Greek uses δικαιοσύνη, which commonly means righteousness or justice. The Hebrew and Greek words do not mean the same thing.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H571. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Hezekiah names this word with peace in Isaiah 39:8. Together they can suggest steady, safe years while he lives.

words.label: Justice
words.meaning: A just decision or the practice of justice.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H4941. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The next commands name the oppressed, the fatherless, and the widow.

words.label: Holy
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H6918. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: In the vision, one calls “Holy” three times. Then he says the LORD’s glory fills the earth.

words.label: Sign
words.greekNote: This form occurs in verses 11 and 14.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H226. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Ahaz will not ask for a sign in verse 12. The Lord gives one in verse 14. Two kings threaten Judah at this time.

words.label: Remnant
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H7605. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The remnant of Jacob will return to the mighty God.

words.label: Shoot
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H2415. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: A shoot comes out of the stock of Jesse. Verse 2 says the LORD’s Spirit will rest on him.

words.label: Salvation
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H3444. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The song joins salvation with trust, strength, and the end of fear.

words.label: Stone
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H68. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God lays this stone in Zion as a sure foundation.

words.label: Book
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H5612. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The vision is like a sealed book that no one can read. The ancient object need not be a bound book.

words.label: Rest
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H5183. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God says returning and rest will save the people. They refuse.

words.label: Wilderness
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H4057. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The wilderness and the dry land will be glad. The desert will blossom like a rose.

words.label: Comfort
words.meaning: To comfort or console in this verse.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H5162. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God gives the command twice: “Comfort, comfort my people.”

words.label: Servant
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H5650. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God says this servant will bring justice to the nations. The word alone does not say who the servant is.

words.label: Redeemed
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H1350. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God tells Israel not to be afraid. He created Israel, called it by name, and says, “You are mine.”

words.label: Anointed
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H4899. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Here the LORD gives the title to Cyrus. The word alone does not make every anointed person the same person.

words.label: Peace
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H7965. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God says the people did not listen to his commandments. If they had, their peace would have been like a river.

words.label: Sickness
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H2483. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The speakers say he bore their sickness. They had thought God struck him. Translations and later readers add to the dictionary meaning.

words.label: Covenant
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H1285. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The mountains may depart and the hills be removed. God’s covenant of peace will not be removed.

words.label: Waters
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H4325. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God invites everyone who thirsts to come to the waters. They may buy wine and milk without money.

words.label: Prayer
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H8605. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God calls his house a house of prayer for all peoples.

words.label: Fast
words.meaning: A fast: a time of going without food.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H6685. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God chooses a fast that lets the oppressed go free. Verse 7 adds bread for the hungry and clothes for the naked.

words.label: Liberty
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H1865. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The speaker is sent to proclaim liberty to the captives. He also preaches good news and binds up the broken hearted.

words.label: New
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H2319. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: God says he creates new heavens and a new earth. The word “new” describes both.

words.label: Spirit
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H7307. The verse may use another form.
