words.discussion: Here it describes a person. God looks to the one who is “poor and of a contrite spirit.”

words.label: King
words.greekNote: The displayed form occurs in verse 1. Verses 16, 17, and 20 use other forms. Verse 6 uses the related verb βασιλεύσομεν.
words.meaning: A king. The chapter names kings of Judah, Syria, Israel, and Assyria.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H4428. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: Kings on both sides of the war have the same title.

words.label: Believe
words.greekNote: This form matches believe. The Greek ends with συνῆτε, meaning understand, where the English has established.
words.meaning: To believe or trust. Another form of the same Hebrew word means to be established.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H539. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The verse uses both forms. Those who will not believe will not be established.

words.label: Virgin / young woman
words.greekNote: The Greek uses παρθένος, commonly translated virgin.
words.meaning: The Hebrew word means a young woman old enough to marry. This English translation uses virgin.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H5959. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The word is part of the sign the Lord gives the house of David. A dictionary alone cannot say who the woman or the child is.

words.label: Immanuel
words.greekNote: The Greek gives the Hebrew name in Greek letters.
words.meaning: The name means God with us.
words.grammar: This is the dictionary form of Hebrew word H6005. The verse may use another form.
words.discussion: The son in the sign receives this name. Two kings threaten Judah at this time.

guides.title: The Assyrian crisis
guides.description: Follow the Assyrian threat from Lachish to Jerusalem.

steps.title: Find the two cities
steps.text: Find Lachish on the map. Rabshakeh, an Assyrian officer, travels from here to Jerusalem. His exact road is unknown.

steps.title: Listen to the argument
steps.text: Rabshakeh mocks Judah’s trust in Egypt and in Hezekiah. What reason does he give against each one?

steps.title: The people on the wall
steps.text: Judah’s officials ask Rabshakeh to speak Aramaic. He shouts to the people on the wall in their own language. Why does he choose that?

steps.title: A threat to move the people
steps.text: Rabshakeh offers food and a new land if the people give up. Yet he will take them from their home. How does he make giving up sound good?

guides.title: Two accounts, one crisis
guides.description: Compare Isaiah’s account with Assyrian records.

steps.title: The palace viewpoint
steps.text: Look at the palace relief. What does it show about the winning king? What does it leave out?

steps.title: The royal inscription
steps.text: Study guide summary: Sennacherib presents Judah’s losses and Hezekiah’s tribute as royal success. The prism does not claim Jerusalem’s capture. Compare this account with Isaiah 37. What does each account emphasize? The photograph shows the Taylor Prism. Luckenbill’s edition translates the separate Chicago Prism.

steps.title: How the account ends
steps.text: Isaiah says the LORD’s angel struck the Assyrian camp and saved Jerusalem. The Assyrian account tells of a royal victory. What does each account want its readers to know?

steps.title: Years between events
steps.text: The last verse tells of Sennacherib’s death many years later. Two verses side by side can be far apart in time.

guides.title: Babylon and Judah’s future
guides.description: Study the events before and after Isaiah 39.

steps.title: A sick king
steps.text: Hezekiah is sick in chapter 38. Verse 6 still promises to defend the city from Assyria. So chapter order may differ from the order of events.

steps.title: Visitors from Babylon
steps.text: Babylon sends visitors to Hezekiah. Their visit’s exact date is uncertain. The map uses 703 BCE to show the setting.

steps.title: Jerusalem’s later destruction
steps.text: Babylon destroys Jerusalem in 587/586 BCE. Isaiah had warned that the palace treasures would go to Babylon. How does the later event fit his warning? Related authorship study: McClellan compares Isaiah 39’s warning with chapter 40’s perspective after exile. His video explains the term Second Isaiah.

steps.title: Persia takes Babylon
steps.text: The timeline ends with Cyrus’s conquest. The Cyrus Cylinder gives a royal account. It does not mention the return of Judah’s exiles.

guides.title: Worship and justice
guides.description: Trace care for vulnerable people across Isaiah.

steps.title: Learn to do good
steps.text: Read Isaiah 1:10–20. Compare the criticism of worship with the command to defend vulnerable people.

steps.title: The vineyard
steps.text: Read Isaiah 5:1–7. Identify the fruit the vineyard owner expected and what he received.

steps.title: The chosen fast
steps.text: Read Isaiah 58:3–12. Name the actions that make worship visible in daily life.

guides.title: Comfort and return
guides.description: Follow images of strength, remembrance, and renewed belonging.

steps.title: Strength for the weary
steps.text: Read Isaiah 40:27–31. Notice how the reply addresses the complaint that God does not see the people.

steps.title: Zion remembered
steps.text: Read Isaiah 49:14–18. Compare Zion’s complaint with the images in God’s answer.

steps.title: A covenant of peace
steps.text: Read Isaiah 54:7–17. Consider how the promise answers abandonment and fear.

guides.title: Read the servant passages
guides.description: Compare the servant’s work, suffering, and vindication.

steps.title: Justice without crushing
steps.text: Read Isaiah 42:1–9. Describe the servant’s task and manner. Keep questions of identity separate from these observations.

steps.title: A wider mission
steps.text: Read Isaiah 49:1–6. Notice how the passage names Israel and also describes restoring Israel.

steps.title: Suffering and vindication
steps.text: Read Isaiah 52:13 through 53:12. Track the speakers and how their view of the servant changes. Compare Christian interpretation in LDS mode.

editorial.status: Complete reading text with original chapter notes. Historical research and language notes remain selected, not exhaustive.
editorial.periodNote: The timeline covers selected events from 780–539 BCE. It does not date every passage. It also does not show every proposed date for when parts of Isaiah were written.
editorial.mapNote: This is a physical reference map. Historical areas and routes use simple shapes. Modern coasts and lakes may differ from ancient ones.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact eighth-century roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Isaiah 36 names travel from Lachish to Jerusalem. It does not identify the chosen road. This route shows one common western approach through the lowlands and hill passes.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact route used in 701 BCE is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its eighth-century path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. It also joined the wider Assyrian road network.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian records and studies of ancient land support this route. It went through the Sajur and Manbij area. It then crossed the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected western lands with the Assyrian heartland. It ended at the capital city of Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip. It crossed the Balih south of Harran. It also crossed Habur streams between Guzana and Nasibina. It then reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers changed mules at road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a broad regional path, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route followed the Tigris. It linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It supported long trips by land and river. Kalhu later became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and their connection are well supported. The line shows a broad route. It does not separate land travel from river travel at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia route
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela. It followed the western edge of the Zagros Mountains. Other routes continued south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The route followed the western edge of the Zagros toward Babylonia. It avoided a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

chapterStudies.context: God refuses their offerings and prayers. Verse 15 gives the reason: their hands are “full of blood.” More worship will not fix this. Verse 17 gives five short commands about other people. Two of them name the fatherless and the widow. Verse 23 says the rulers love bribes and do not hear the widow’s case. So justice here means fair courts, not only kind acts.
chapterStudies.text: Learn to do well. Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed. Defend the fatherless. Plead for the widow.”

chapterStudies.context: Why do the nations stop fighting? Verse 3 says they come to learn the LORD’s ways. Verse 4 says he judges between them. A judge they all accept ends the need for war. So the metal for swords can become farm tools. Verses 7–8 show the contrast in Judah now: horses, chariots, and idols. Peace here comes from accepting a judge, not from stronger armies.
chapterStudies.text: He will judge between the nations, and will decide concerning many peoples. They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 1–7 show a city with no one fit to lead. Verse 14 gives the reason. The leaders have “eaten up the vineyard,” and stolen goods fill their houses. Verse 15 is the LORD’s question to them as judge. To “grind the face of the poor” pictures a millstone on grain. The poor are treated like something to be used up. So the loss of leaders is a sentence, not bad luck.
chapterStudies.text: What do you mean that you crush my people, and grind the face of the poor?” says the Lord, GOD of Armies.

chapterStudies.context: Shelter comes last in this chapter, after the washing in verse 4. The city is cleaned before it is covered. Verse 5 uses cloud by day and fire by night. Exodus 13:21 uses the same pair for Israel’s travel through the wilderness. Here the cloud and fire stay over one city and its meetings. Verse 6 adds plain needs: shade, refuge, and cover from rain. So the promise is safety for people who came through the judgment.
chapterStudies.text: There will be a pavilion for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a refuge and for a shelter from storm and from rain.

chapterStudies.context: The song works like a trap. In verse 3 the hearers are asked to judge a bad vineyard. Verse 7 then tells them they are the vineyard. The owner did all the work in verse 2, so the vines have no excuse. He looked for justice and found oppression. He looked for right living and heard a cry. The woes in verses 8–23 list what the wild grapes are.
chapterStudies.text: For the vineyard of the LORD of Armies is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant. He looked for justice, but behold, oppression, for righteousness, but behold, a cry of distress.

chapterStudies.context: Isaiah can answer only after verse 7. In verse 5 he says his lips are unclean. A coal from the altar touches his lips, and his sin is taken away. Then he hears the question and says, “Send me.” The Lord does not name Isaiah or order him. Isaiah offers before he hears the task. Verses 9–12 then tell him that most people will not listen.
chapterStudies.text: I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”

chapterStudies.context: Verse 9 states the test for Ahaz. The lists in verses 8–9 name each enemy capital and its king. They are only men in two cities. Then the verse turns to Ahaz: without belief, he will not stand. Ahaz refuses a sign in verse 12 and sounds careful. Isaiah calls it trying God’s patience. Verse 17 shows the cost: Assyria comes to Judah.
chapterStudies.text: The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son. If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.’ ”

chapterStudies.context: Judah’s people fear a plot by two kings (7:2). Verse 12 tells Isaiah not to use their word for it or share their fear. Verse 13 gives the other choice: fear the LORD of Armies. Verse 14 says he will be a holy place or a stone that trips. The same God is safety for one group and a trap for another. The difference is whom each group fears. Verse 19 shows where the wrong fear leads: asking the dead.
chapterStudies.text: “Don’t call a conspiracy all that this people call a conspiracy. Don’t fear their threats or be terrorized.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 4–5 end a war. Verse 7 says what replaces it. The child’s rule and its peace keep growing without end. He sits on David’s throne, so the promise is about David’s royal line. He holds the kingdom up with justice and right living. Chapter 1 asked Jerusalem’s rulers for the same two things. The last line names who makes it happen: the zeal of the LORD of Armies.
chapterStudies.text: Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on David’s throne, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of the LORD of Armies will perform this.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 5 calls Assyria a rod in the LORD’s hand. In verse 13 the king says his own hand and wisdom did it. Verse 15 answers with tools: an ax, a saw, a rod, a staff. A tool does not move by itself and cannot boast over its user. Verse 7 explains the gap: the king means to destroy, not to correct. So the LORD can use Assyria and still punish its pride (verse 12).
chapterStudies.text: Should an ax brag against him who chops with it? Should a saw exalt itself above him who saws with it? As if a rod should lift those who lift it up, or as if a staff should lift up someone who is not wood.

chapterStudies.context: Jesse was David’s father, so the shoot is a new king from David’s family. Verse 3 says how he will not judge: by looks or by talk. Looks and talk can hide who is in the right. Verse 4 gives the result: the poor and the humble get fair rulings. His weapon is his mouth, so he rules by what he says. The peace among animals in verses 6–9 follows this fair judging. Verse 9 gives the cause: the earth is full of knowing the LORD.
chapterStudies.text: but he will judge the poor with righteousness, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.

chapterStudies.context: The song answers chapters 1–11. Verse 1 looks back at the anger those chapters describe. Verse 2 says, “I will trust, and will not be afraid.” Ahaz was asked for that trust in chapter 7 and refused. Verse 3 turns salvation into water drawn from a well. A well gives water every day, not once. Verses 4–5 then send the news out to all the peoples.
chapterStudies.text: Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 11 is the LORD’s own reason for the army in verses 2–5. He names two targets: evil and pride. The chapter is titled for Babylon, but this verse says “the world.” Babylon stands as the chief example, “the glory of kingdoms” in verse 19. The Medes in verse 17 cannot be paid to stop. So wealth, Babylon’s strength, gives no way out. The empty city in verses 20–22 shows pride brought down to nothing.
chapterStudies.text: I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity. I will cause the arrogance of the proud to cease, and will humble the arrogance of the terrible.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 3 sets the time: after the LORD gives rest from hard service. Only then can former slaves sing against their master. Verse 4 calls the song a “parable,” a poem with a point. Its first word about the king is “oppressor.” The song then follows him down: from throne, to Sheol, to no grave. His boast in verses 13–14 goes up five times with “I will.” Verse 15 answers with one line going down.
chapterStudies.text: that you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and say, “How the oppressor has ceased! The golden city has ceased!”

chapterStudies.context: Verses 1–4 list Moab’s towns as they fall and weep. Verse 5 breaks the list with the speaker’s own feeling. Moab is a foreign nation, yet the speaker grieves. The verse then follows real people on a road: uphill at Luhith, then toward Horonaim. Naming each climb slows the reader to walking speed. The message judges Moab without enjoying its pain. Chapter 16:11 repeats this grief.
chapterStudies.text: My heart cries out for Moab! Her nobles flee to Zoar, to Eglath Shelishiyah; for they go up by the ascent of Luhith with weeping; for on the way to Horonaim, they raise up a cry of destruction.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 3–4 ask someone to hide Moab’s outcasts from the destroyer. Verse 1 points the request to Mount Zion. Verse 5 gives the reason Zion can be asked. A throne there will be set up in loving kindness, and its judge seeks justice. So the shelter depends on a just ruler, not on strong walls. Verse 6 shows what blocks it: Moab’s pride. The text does not say whether the shelter is given.
chapterStudies.text: Let my outcasts dwell with you! As for Moab, be a hiding place for him from the face of the destroyer. For the extortionist is brought to nothing. Destruction ceases. The oppressors are consumed out of the land.

chapterStudies.context: The chapter joins Damascus and Ephraim because they were allies (7:2). Both are stripped. Verse 6 leaves only a few olives after the tree is shaken. Verse 7 says what the few who remain will do: look to their Maker. Verse 8 names what they stop looking to: altars and poles their own fingers made. The contrast is between the one who made them and things they made. Verse 10 gives the cause of the loss: they forgot God.
chapterStudies.text: In that day, people will look to their Maker, and their eyes will have respect for the Holy One of Israel.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 2 and verse 7 describe the same people in the same words. In verse 2 messengers go out to them. In verse 7 they come to Mount Zion with a gift. Between the two, the LORD does nothing loud. Verse 4 says he stays still and watches. Verse 5 says he cuts at the right time, before harvest. So the chapter moves a far, feared nation from sending messengers to bringing a gift.
chapterStudies.text: In that time, a present will be brought to the LORD of Armies from a people tall and smooth, even from a people awesome from their beginning onward, a nation that measures out and treads down, whose land the rivers divide, to the place of the name of the LORD of Armies, Mount Zion.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 25 gives Egypt and Assyria names once used for Israel. Egypt is “my people.” Assyria is “the work of my hands.” Israel keeps “my inheritance” and is counted third (verse 24). Egypt once held Israel as slaves, and Assyria is the rod of chapter 10. Verse 22 explains the change: the LORD strikes in order to heal. So the judgment in verses 1–17 is not the last word for Israel’s enemies.
chapterStudies.text: because the LORD of Armies has blessed them, saying, “Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.”

chapterStudies.context: Isaiah’s body is the message here. For three years people see what a prisoner of war looks like. Verse 4 says Egypt and Ethiopia will walk that way behind Assyria’s king. Verse 5 turns to those who watched: they hoped in Ethiopia and boasted in Egypt. Verse 6 has the coast people say, “This is our expectation.” The sign shows them their helper as a captive. The chapter ends on their question, with no answer given.
chapterStudies.text: They will be dismayed and confounded, because of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 15 says why the travelers need help: they ran from swords and bows. Verse 14 shows the people of Tema meeting them with water and bread. The text gives no order from God for this help. It reports what neighbors did for the thirsty. Verse 13 says the caravans must sleep in the thickets. Verses 16–17 then say Kedar’s fighters will become few. So the small kindness sits inside a short, hard warning.
chapterStudies.text: They brought water to him who was thirsty. The inhabitants of the land of Tema met the fugitives with their bread.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 8–11 list sensible work for a city under attack. They check armor, fix walls, and save water. None of that is blamed. The blame comes in verse 11: they did not look to the LORD. Verse 12 says he called for weeping. Verse 13 shows a party in its place. So the fault is acting as if the danger had no author and no message.
chapterStudies.text: You also made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool. But you didn’t look to him who had done this, neither did you have respect for him who planned it long ago.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 8 asks a question, and verse 9 answers it. The question lists Tyre’s honors: it gave crowns, and its traders were princes. No army is named as the cause. The answer names the LORD and his aim: to bring pride into contempt. This matches 2:12, where a day comes against all that is proud. Verse 18 shows the aim was not to end trade. The same earnings later buy food and clothing for those who live before the LORD.
chapterStudies.text: The LORD of Armies has planned it, to stain the pride of all glory, to bring into contempt all the honorable of the earth.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 1–4 describe a ruined earth. Verse 5 gives the reason, and it is about people, not nature. They broke laws, statutes, and “the everlasting covenant.” The verse says the earth is polluted “under its inhabitants.” The land carries the cost of what people do on it. Verse 2 shows that rank gives no escape. Verse 6 draws the line from cause to result with the word “Therefore.”
chapterStudies.text: The earth also is polluted under its inhabitants, because they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, and broken the everlasting covenant.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 6 sets a table for all peoples. Verse 7 says a covering lies over every nation. Verse 8 then names death. In 5:14 Sheol opens its mouth and people go down into it. Here the LORD swallows death. Then he wipes the tears from all faces. Verse 9 gives the guests’ answer: they waited, and he saved them.
chapterStudies.text: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for the LORD has spoken it.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 18 is the low point of the song. The people worked like a woman in labor and produced only wind. They saved no one. Verse 14 said of the other lords, “The dead shall not live.” Verse 19 turns that line around for the LORD’s people: “Your dead shall live.” The cause is “your dew,” something that comes from God, not from their work. So life comes where their own effort failed.
chapterStudies.text: Your dead shall live. Their dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

chapterStudies.context: This song answers the vineyard song in chapter 5. There the owner removed the wall and held back rain (5:5–6). Here the LORD guards the vineyard night and day and waters it (verse 3). There it gave wild grapes. Here Israel fills the world with fruit. Verse 9 says what changed: the altars and poles are broken, and sin is forgiven. So the fruit follows the removal of the idols.
chapterStudies.text: In days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will blossom and bud. They will fill the surface of the world with fruit.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 15 gives the rulers’ boast. They made a deal with death, so the flood will pass them by. The verse has them call their own shelter “lies.” Verse 16 is the LORD’s answer: a tested stone, laid by him, in Zion. One who believes “shall not act hastily,” so trust replaces panic. Verse 17 checks every wall against justice and righteousness. Verse 18 cancels the deal with death.
chapterStudies.text: Therefore the Lord GOD says, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 1 lets the feasts “come around” year after year. Worship in Ariel has not stopped. Verse 13 names the fault: lips are near, and the heart is far. Their fear of God is “a commandment of men which has been taught.” It is learned by rule, not meant. Verses 11–12 show the result: no one can read the vision, schooled or not. Verse 18 undoes it when the deaf hear the book’s words.
chapterStudies.text: The Lord said, “Because this people draws near with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught;

chapterStudies.context: Verse 15 sets two plans side by side. The LORD’s plan is to return, rest, stay quiet, and trust. Judah’s plan in verse 16 is fast horses, which Egypt supplies (31:1). The verse ends with two words: “You refused.” Verse 16 turns their plan around: they will flee, and the chasers will be fast. Verse 18 then uses “wait” for both sides. The LORD waits to be gracious, and those who wait for him are blessed.
chapterStudies.text: For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” You refused,

chapterStudies.context: Verse 1 gives Judah’s reason: Egypt’s chariots are many and its horsemen strong. Verse 3 answers with two plain pairs. Egyptians are men, not God. Horses are flesh, not spirit. The count of chariots does not change what they are made of. Then one hand moves, and both the helper and the helped fall. Verse 8 adds that Assyria will fall by a sword “not of man.”
chapterStudies.text: Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, both he who helps shall stumble, and he who is helped shall fall, and they all shall be consumed together.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 17 says where peace comes from. It is “the work of righteousness,” so it is a result, not a starting point. Verses 9–11 show another calm: women at ease before the harvest fails. Their ease rests on a good year. The peace in verse 17 follows the Spirit (verse 15) and justice (verse 16). Verse 18 gives it a home: safe houses and quiet resting places. Verse 19 says it holds even when hail flattens the forest.
chapterStudies.text: The work of righteousness will be peace, and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 14 asks who can live near the LORD’s fire. Verses 15–16 answer with a person who is honest and takes no bribe. Verse 22 then says why the city is safe. It gives the LORD three offices: judge, lawgiver, and king. Chapters 1 and 3 blamed Judah’s human judges and rulers. Here the LORD holds all three jobs himself. So the last line, “He will save us,” rests on who rules.
chapterStudies.text: For the LORD is our judge. The LORD is our lawgiver. The LORD is our king. He will save us.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 1–7 describe a slaughter without giving a reason. Verse 8 gives it: this is “for the cause of Zion.” “Cause” here means a case to be settled. So the violence is presented as a judge’s payment, not as rage alone. Edom is the one nation named beside “all the nations” in verse 2. Verses 11–17 hand its land to wild animals by measuring line. Chapter 35 then shows the other side of the same day for Zion.
chapterStudies.text: For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.

chapterStudies.context: Chapter 34 turned a nation’s land into desert. Chapter 35 turns desert into a garden with a road. Verse 10 says who uses the road: “the LORD’s ransomed ones.” A ransom is a price paid to free someone. They return as freed people. Verses 8–9 make the road safe: no unclean traveler, no lion. The verse ends with joy on their heads and sorrow running away.
chapterStudies.text: Then the LORD’s ransomed ones will return, and come with singing to Zion; and everlasting joy will be on their heads. They will obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.”

chapterStudies.context: Rabshakeh’s speech takes away each thing Judah might trust. Verse 6 starts with Egypt, a reed that breaks and stabs the hand. Isaiah gave the same warning in chapters 30 and 31. So the enemy is right on this point. Verse 7 attacks trust in the LORD. Verse 10 claims the LORD sent Assyria. The speech mixes true warning with false claims, and the people stay silent (verse 21).
chapterStudies.text: Behold, you trust in the staff of this bruised reed, even in Egypt, which if a man leans on it, it will go into his hand and pierce it. So is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.

chapterStudies.context: Hezekiah’s prayer agrees with part of the letter. Verse 18 admits that Assyria did destroy those lands. Verse 19 gives the reason their gods fell: they were wood and stone. Verse 16 sets the LORD apart as maker of heaven and earth. Then verse 20 asks for rescue and gives a purpose. All kingdoms should know that the LORD alone is God. The request rests on God’s name, not on Judah’s merit.
chapterStudies.text: Now therefore, LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you are the LORD, even you only.”

chapterStudies.context: The poem has two halves. Verses 10–14 speak from inside the sickness, with a tent pulled down. Verse 15 is the turn: God has spoken and done it. Verse 16 then says people live “by these things.” The nearest match is God’s word and act in verse 15. So Hezekiah counts his life as given back, not earned. Verses 18–19 give the reason it matters: only the living can praise.
chapterStudies.text: Lord, men live by these things; and my spirit finds life in all of them. You restore me, and cause me to live.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 2 says Hezekiah left nothing unshown. Verse 6 answers in the same terms: nothing will be left. The list of what he showed becomes the list of what Babylon takes. In chapters 36–38 the danger was Assyria. This verse names Babylon as the one who will empty the palace. Verse 8 gives Hezekiah’s reply: peace “in my days.” The chapter leaves the reader with his children’s days still to come.
chapterStudies.text: ‘Behold, the days are coming when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up until today, will be carried to Babylon. Nothing will be left,’ says the LORD.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 27 quotes the complaint this chapter answers. Jacob says his way is hidden and his case ignored. Verses 12–26 have already shown God’s size against seas, nations, and stars. Verse 28 turns that size toward the tired. The Creator does not faint, and no one can search out his understanding. So he is neither too weak to help nor unaware. Verse 29 says where his strength goes: to the weak.
chapterStudies.text: Haven’t you known? Haven’t you heard? The everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint. He isn’t weary. His understanding is unsearchable.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 5–7 show how the nations meet fear. They cheer each other on and nail an idol so it will not totter. Verse 10 shows how Israel is to meet the same fear. The reasons are two short facts: “I am with you” and “I am your God.” Three promises follow: strengthen, help, uphold. The nations hold their god up. Israel’s God holds Israel up with his right hand.
chapterStudies.text: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 1 gives the servant a large task: justice for the nations. Verses 2–3 say how he does it. He is quiet, and he is careful with what is nearly finished. A bruised reed is bent, and a dim wick is almost out. He does not snap one or snuff the other. Rabshakeh used a “bruised reed” for a useless ally in 36:6. Here the weak are the ones the servant protects while he brings justice.
chapterStudies.text: He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick. He will faithfully bring justice.

chapterStudies.context: The verse opens with “But now,” so it answers the end of chapter 42. There Israel was burned and did not understand (42:25). Here the same people are told not to fear. Three reasons follow: “I have redeemed,” “I have called,” and “You are mine.” To call by name is to claim one person, not a crowd. Verse 2 does not remove water or fire. It promises company through them.
chapterStudies.text: But now the LORD who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel, says: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 24–28 are one long sentence about what the LORD says and does. It starts with making heaven and earth. It ends with one man’s name: Cyrus. The LORD calls him “my shepherd” and says he will do all the LORD wants. His job is stated at once: Jerusalem built and the temple’s base laid. Verses 9–20 showed gods who cannot speak. Here the LORD names a ruler and says what he will do.
chapterStudies.text: who says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure,’ even saying of Jerusalem, ‘She will be built;’ and of the temple, ‘Your foundation will be laid.’ ”

chapterStudies.context: “Anointed” is the word for Israel’s own kings and priests. Verse 1 gives it to Cyrus, a foreign king. Verses 4 and 5 both say Cyrus has not known the LORD. So the title describes a task, not his faith. Verse 4 also gives the reason: “for Jacob my servant’s sake.” Verses 9–10 expect people to object to this choice. The answer is the potter’s right over the clay.
chapterStudies.text: The LORD says to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have held to subdue nations before him and strip kings of their armor, to open the doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut:

chapterStudies.context: The chapter turns on one verb: carry. In verses 1–2 tired animals carry gods that cannot save the load. In verse 7 people carry a god on their shoulders. In verses 3–4 the LORD carries his people from the womb to gray hair. A made god must be carried. The God who made them does the carrying. Verse 4 puts it plainly: “I have made, and I will bear.”
chapterStudies.text: Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear. Yes, I will carry, and will deliver.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 10 quotes Babylon’s thoughts twice. First: “No one sees me.” Then: “I am, and there is no one else besides me.” The LORD says the second line of himself in 45:5–6. So Babylon claims God’s place in God’s words. Verse 6 shows what that belief allowed: no mercy for captives or the old. Verse 11 answers “No one sees” with a disaster she will not see coming.
chapterStudies.text: For you have trusted in your wickedness. You have said, ‘No one sees me.’ Your wisdom and your knowledge has perverted you. You have said in your heart, ‘I am, and there is no one else besides me.’

chapterStudies.context: Verses 1–19 are hard on Israel: stubborn, late to listen, tested in a furnace. Verse 20 still tells them to go free. The reason was given in verses 9 and 11: “for my own sake.” The rescue does not wait for Israel to deserve it. They are to leave shouting, so the far earth hears who redeemed them. Verse 21 recalls water from the rock in the first desert journey. Verse 22 keeps the warning: the wicked have no peace.
chapterStudies.text: Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! With the sound of joyful shouting announce this, tell it even to the end of the earth; say, “The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!”

chapterStudies.context: Verse 13 calls heaven and earth to sing because the LORD has comforted his people. Verse 14 cuts in with Zion’s own voice: “forsaken” and “forgotten.” Verse 15 answers with the closest bond the speaker can name. A nursing mother can hardly forget her child. Then it allows that even she may. The LORD’s memory is set above the strongest human one. Verse 16 adds that Zion is engraved on the palms of his hands.
chapterStudies.text: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!

chapterStudies.context: Verse 2 asked why no one answered when the LORD called. Verse 4 shows one who does. His ear is woken every morning, so he listens before he speaks. His tongue is “taught,” and its use is to hold up the weary. Verse 5 says he did not turn back from what he heard. Verse 6 shows the cost: beating, pulled beard, spitting. Verse 7 gives his reason for standing: the Lord GOD will help.
chapterStudies.text: The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 1–2 give the proof before the promise. Abraham was one man, and a nation came from him and Sarah. Verse 3 applies that to Zion’s ruins. If God made many from one, he can make a garden from a waste. The verse names Eden, the first garden. The result is heard, not only seen: joy, thanks, and song. Verse 12 names the speaker’s role in one phrase: “he who comforts you.”
chapterStudies.text: For the LORD has comforted Zion. He has comforted all her waste places, and has made her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the LORD. Joy and gladness will be found in them, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 7 looks at a runner’s feet because the news depends on his arrival. A city under threat waits for word from outside. In verse 8 the watchmen sing when they see the LORD return. The message has four parts: good news, peace, salvation, and “Your God reigns!” The last part explains the first three. Verse 5 said foreign rulers mock God’s name. The runner tells Zion who rules now.
chapterStudies.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news, who proclaims salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

chapterStudies.context: Verse 4 holds two views of the same suffering. The second half is what the speakers once thought: God was striking him. The first half is what they now say: the sickness and pain were theirs. The word “Surely” marks the change of mind. Verse 5 repeats it four ways: pierced, crushed, punished, wounded, each “for our” wrongs. Verse 6 says why: all of them went astray like sheep. The chapter does not name the servant, and readers have identified him in different ways.
chapterStudies.text: Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 7–8 set a short moment of anger against lasting kindness. Verse 9 ties the promise to the oath after Noah’s flood. Verse 10 then picks the steadiest things a person can see: mountains and hills. Even those may move. Two things will not: his loving kindness and his “covenant of peace.” The speaker is named as “the LORD who has mercy on you.” So the promise rests on his character, not on the wife’s record.
chapterStudies.text: For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed, but my loving kindness will not depart from you, and my covenant of peace will not be removed,” says the LORD who has mercy on you.

chapterStudies.context: The verse sounds like a seller calling in a market. But the price is removed: “without money and without price.” The word “buy” stays, so the goods are real and must still be taken. Verse 2 names the other choice: paying for what does not feed. Verse 3 says what the food is: listening, which gives life. Verse 7 shows who may come: even the wicked, who will be freely pardoned. So the only need is thirst and a willingness to come.
chapterStudies.text: “Hey! Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 3 names two who expect to be shut out: the foreigner and the eunuch. Each fear is quoted. Both get the same test: keep the Sabbath and hold the covenant. Verse 7 then gives the foreigner full access: the mountain, the house, and the altar. Their offerings “will be accepted.” The reason is the name of the house itself: prayer “for all peoples.” Verse 8 adds that God will gather still others.
chapterStudies.text: I will bring these to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer. Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

chapterStudies.context: The verse gives God two addresses. One is “the high and holy place.” The other is with a person who is sorry and humble. Verse 7 showed people climbing a high mountain to reach their gods. Here the high God comes down to the low. His purpose is stated twice: to revive. Verse 16 gives his reason for ending anger: the people he made would faint.
chapterStudies.text: For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 3 gives the people’s complaint: they fast, and God does not notice. The same verse gives his answer: they oppress their workers that very day. Verses 6–7 then define the fast with actions toward others. Verse 7 moves close to home: your bread, your house, “your own flesh.” The hungry and the naked are treated as family. Verses 8–9 attach the answer to prayer to this fast. Chapter 1 made the same link between worship and justice.
chapterStudies.text: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?

chapterStudies.context: Verse 1 says the LORD is able to save. Verses 2–8 say why he has not: the people’s own violence and lies. In verses 9–15 they confess it in their own voice. Verse 16 comes after that confession. He looks for a human to step in and finds none. So he acts himself, with his own arm. Verse 20 names who receives it: those who turn from disobedience.
chapterStudies.text: He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no intercessor. Therefore his own arm brought salvation to him; and his righteousness sustained him.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 2 sets the scene: darkness over all the peoples, light on one city. Verse 3 gives the result. Nations walk toward the only light they can see. The light is not Zion’s own, since verse 1 calls it “the LORD’s glory.” Chapter 2:2–3 pictured nations going up to learn. Here they come because of what they see. Verse 19 names the source: the LORD is her light.
chapterStudies.text: Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

chapterStudies.context: The speaker gives his authority first: the Spirit and an anointing. Then he lists whom he is sent to. Each is someone in loss: the humble, the broken hearted, captives, the bound. His tools are words: preach, proclaim, comfort. Verse 3 turns those words into exchanges, such as a garland for ashes. Verse 4 shows the helped people at work, rebuilding ruins. Luke 4:16–21 reports Jesus reading this passage in the Nazareth synagogue.
chapterStudies.text: The Lord GOD’s Spirit is on me, because the LORD has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and release to those who are bound,

chapterStudies.context: The verse works by replacing names. The old ones are “Forsaken” and “Desolate.” Zion said “forsaken” of herself in 49:14. Hephzibah goes with “the LORD delights in you.” Beulah goes with “your land will be married.” So the names record a changed relationship, not a changed place. Verse 12 ends the chapter with one more name: “A City Not Forsaken.”
chapterStudies.text: You will not be called Forsaken any more, nor will your land be called Desolate any more; but you will be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for the LORD delights in you, and your land will be married.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 1–6 show God as a lone warrior. Verse 9 shows the same God from the side of his people. Their pain is said to be his: “he was afflicted.” Then come four acts: saved, redeemed, bore, carried. Verse 10 follows with “But they rebelled,” so the care came first. The prayer in verses 15–17 leans on this memory. It asks the one who carried them to look again.
chapterStudies.text: In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them. In his love and in his pity he redeemed them. He bore them, and carried them all the days of old.

chapterStudies.context: Verses 5–7 leave the people with nothing to offer. Their best acts are unclean, and no one even prays. Verse 8 begins “But now” and changes the ground of the request. They do not point to themselves. They point to what God is to them: Father and potter. Clay has no claim except that the potter made it. Verse 9 draws the request from that: “we are all your people.”
chapterStudies.text: But now, LORD, you are our Father. We are the clay and you our potter. We all are the work of your hand.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 17 uses “create,” the verb of Genesis 1:1, for something new. The next lines keep the new world close to daily life. Verses 21–22 promise that builders live in their houses and planters eat their fruit. That reverses 1:7, where strangers ate the land. Verse 19 ends the weeping, and verse 20 ends early death. So the new earth is described by which losses stop. Verse 25 repeats the peaceful animals of 11:6–9.
chapterStudies.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things will not be remembered, nor come into mind.

chapterStudies.context: Verse 1 asks what house could hold the one who made everything. Verse 2 says where he looks instead: to a kind of person. Three marks are given: poor, sorry for wrong, and trembling at his word. Verse 3 shows the opposite: people who make offerings but “have chosen their own ways.” Their ox and lamb count as crimes. So the book ends where it began in chapter 1. Worship is weighed by the worshiper’s heart and conduct.
chapterStudies.text: For my hand has made all these things, and so all these things came to be,” says the LORD: “but I will look to this man, even to he who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.
